title: Universal State Merging For Almost I.i.d. States
authors: Nilanjana Datta
abstract: ArXiv:2611.32065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In quantum state merging, Alice aims to transfer her share of a bipartite state to Bob while preserving the joint state with a purifying reference. For i.i.d. copies of [MATH], the optimal asymptotic net entanglement cost is [MATH] ebits per pair. We show that this cost is robust under deviations from exact i.i.d. structure. For every [MATH], a single sequence of one-way LOCC protocols, depending only on [MATH] and [MATH], merges every weakly almost i.i.d. source along [MATH] with vanishing error. The net entanglement cost is at most [MATH] ebits for all sufficiently large blocklengths [MATH]. This guarantee also covers the Wasserstein and Mazzola--Sutter--Renner subclasses. Each class contains the exact i.i.d. source, so [MATH] is optimal for universal merging within each class. More generally, the same protocols achieve vanishing error whenever the two-pair marginal of the permutation-averaged source converges in trace norm to [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves universal one-way LOCC state-merging protocols for weakly almost i.i.d. bipartite quantum sources with asymptotically optimal net entanglement cost.
motivation: Quantum state merging is a central primitive in quantum information, and its standard optimal entanglement cost is known for exact i.i.d. sources; this work asks whether that cost remains achievable under realistic deviations from exact i.i.d. structure.
method: The author constructs a single sequence of one-way LOCC protocols, depending only on the almost-i.i.d. class parameters, and analyzes permutation-averaged sources and their two-pair marginals to establish vanishing-error merging guarantees.
result: For every weakly almost i.i.d. source, the protocols merge the state with vanishing error at net entanglement cost at most the i.i.d. optimal rate for sufficiently large blocklengths, covering Wasserstein and Mazzola-Sutter-Renner subclasses and establishing optimality within each class.
conclusion: The optimal asymptotic entanglement cost of quantum state merging is robust beyond exact i.i.d. assumptions, and a unified protocol achieves universal merging whenever the permutation-averaged two-pair marginal converges in trace norm.

title: Spinal Reflected Entropy Reveals Logical Magic
authors: Zong-Yue Hou, Yuzhen Zhang, Zhi-Cheng Yang, Yingfei Gu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement and magic are usually regarded as independent quantum resources. Here we connect the two in the toric code, where the stabilizer R\'enyi entropy of the stored logical state, a widely used measure of magic, acquires a direct interpretation in terms of entanglement. We introduce the spinal reflected entropy, defined on a neighborhood of a spine of the underlying surface as the reflected entropy between a disk around the vertex of the spine and bands along its noncontractible loops. It obeys an area law with a topological correction and contains one additional term that carries all the dependence on the stored state. On a torus, this term equals the stabilizer R\'enyi entropy of the stored state plus the logarithm of the ground-state degeneracy. The mechanism is topological. On the surface sewn to its reflected copy, the bands close into tubes, logical Pauli operators become anyon charges threading them, and these charges are distributed as the outcomes of Bell sampling of the stored state. The result extends to surfaces of higher genus and to general two-dimensional topological stabilizer codes on qubits. Logical magic thus becomes a geometrically defined entanglement quantity, one that shallow circuits preserving the code space cannot change.
tldr: The paper shows that in the toric code, the magic of a stored logical state—measured by stabilizer Rényi entropy—is encoded in a geometrically defined entanglement quantity called spinal reflected entropy.
motivation: Entanglement and magic are typically treated as independent quantum resources, but this work aims to connect them by giving logical magic a direct entanglement interpretation in topological stabilizer codes.
method: The authors define spinal reflected entropy on a neighborhood of a spine of the underlying surface, using reflected entropy between a disk around a spine vertex and bands along noncontractible loops, and analyze its behavior in the toric code and higher-genus/general 2D topological stabilizer codes.
result: The spinal reflected entropy obeys an area law with a topological correction, and its state-dependent term equals the stabilizer Rényi entropy of the stored logical state plus the logarithm of the ground-state degeneracy on a torus.
conclusion: Logical magic becomes a geometrically defined entanglement quantity in topological codes, invariant under shallow circuits preserving the code space, thereby linking magic and entanglement resources.

The authors consider a toric code on a torus and define a spine—a graph embedded on the surface—and take a neighborhood of it. They then compute the reflected entropy between a disk around a vertex of the spine and bands along the noncontractible loops of the spine. This quantity is shown to obey an area law with a topological correction and to contain an additional term that depends on the stored logical state. Specifically, on a torus, this term equals the stabilizer Rényi entropy of the stored state plus the logarithm of the ground-state degeneracy. The mechanism is topological: on the surface sewn to its reflected copy, the bands close into tubes, logical Pauli operators become anyon charges threading these tubes, and these charges are distributed as the outcomes of Bell sampling of the stored state. The result extends to higher-genus surfaces and to general two-dimensional topological stabilizer codes on qubits. The authors argue that logical magic thus becomes a geometrically defined entanglement quantity that shallow circuits preserving the code space cannot change.

By analyzing the resulting entanglement structure, they derive an area law with a topological correction and isolate the state-dependent term. The key technical step involves sewing the surface to its reflected copy, which transforms the bands into tubes and maps logical Pauli operators to anyon charges threading these tubes. This mapping allows them to relate the entanglement quantity to the stabilizer Rényi entropy via the distribution of anyon charges, which they identify with Bell sampling outcomes. The analysis is analytical and relies on properties of topological stabilizer codes and anyon models. The extension to higher genus and general 2D topological stabilizer codes is argued by generalizing the topological mechanism.

The authors show that this term arises from the distribution of anyon charges threading the tubes, which corresponds to Bell sampling outcomes. This provides an operational interpretation: the magic of the logical state is encoded in the entanglement between the disk and the bands. title: Certifying Closed Labs In Device-independent Tests Of Indefinite Causality
authors: Hannah Seabrook, Fabio Costa, Paul Skrzypczyk, Giulia Rubino
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Indefinite causal order allows processes in which the order of events is not predetermined, enabling information-processing advantages unattainable with fixed causal structures. A long-standing open problem is whether such processes can be certified without trusting the devices used to demonstrate them, analogous to device-independent certifications of Bell nonlocality. Causal inequalities offer a route towards this goal, since their violation is intended to rule out all definite causal structures. However, fully device-independent certification of indefinite causal order remains elusive. The difficulty lies in the closed laboratories assumption, which requires each party to interact at most once with systems that mediate communication. Without this assumption, ordinary two-way communication can reproduce causal-inequality violations without involving indefinite causal order. Yet an untrusted device could violate the assumption by interacting with the mediating system more than once, while remaining undetected from input-output statistics alone. We address this loophole by embedding a minimal set of additional experimental components into a certification scheme. These elements probabilistically probe the underlying process, enabling the closed laboratories assumption to be validated directly within the protocol. Our framework provides operationally meaningful minimal-assumption tests of indefinite causal order, clarifying its distinction from nonlocality and paving the way for cryptographic and self-testing applications.
tldr: The paper proposes a certification scheme for indefinite causal order that validates the closed-laboratories assumption using minimal additional experimental components, moving toward device-independent tests of indefinite causality.
motivation: Device-independent certification of indefinite causal order is a long-standing open problem, and causal-inequality violations alone can be mimicked by ordinary two-way communication if the closed-laboratories assumption is violated by untrusted devices.
method: The authors embed a minimal set of additional components into a causal-inequality certification protocol; these components probabilistically probe the underlying process so that the closed-laboratories assumption can be checked directly within the protocol.
result: The framework enables operationally meaningful minimal-assumption tests of indefinite causal order and clarifies how it differs from nonlocality, while avoiding the loophole where an untrusted device interacts multiple times with the mediating system undetected.
conclusion: This provides a route toward fully device-independent certification of indefinite causal order and opens the door to cryptographic and self-testing applications based on indefinite causality.

However, their violation can be mimicked by ordinary two-way communication if the closed laboratories assumption is not enforced. This assumption requires that each party interacts at most once with the mediating system. The authors propose a solution by embedding additional experimental components that probabilistically probe the underlying process, thereby validating the closed laboratories assumption within the protocol itself. This enables operationally meaningful minimal-assumption tests of ICO. The work clarifies the distinction between ICO and nonlocality and paves the way for cryptographic and self-testing applications. The paper includes theoretical analysis and supplementary materials with figures, though specific numerical results are not detailed in the abstract.

title: Hybrid Correlation Generation With Finite Shared Randomness
authors: Zihan Chen, Shengjun Wu, Zeng-Bing Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finite shared randomness can reduce the use of a prescribed two-qubit source in a hybrid model. Each party has two fixed binary projective measurements, and the protocol reproduces the resulting joint outcome distributions exactly. The parties choose their classical or quantum interfaces independently, without using the shared label, and keep their classical response functions fixed across branches. Eight labels suffice to preserve all feasible pairs of interface choice probabilities, and this bound is tight. The known classical four-label bound yields minimum-cost saturation. With an unrestricted label budget, the minimum source cost is zero if the target can be reproduced by a purely classical protocol, and one otherwise. For Werner states with identical orthogonal measurement pairs, the exact minimum source cost is obtained for every label budget. The three-label cost jumps at visibility [MATH]. Four labels give zero cost at every visibility. In a family of separable states, the two-label cost varies nonmonotonically with local bias while the full correlation tensor remains fixed. The distributed sampling analysis gives the minimum source cost at each label budget and the minimum worst-case total variation error for classical protocols with at most two shared labels.
tldr: The paper analyzes the minimum cost of a prescribed two-qubit quantum source for exactly reproducing joint outcome distributions in a hybrid classical-quantum model with finite shared randomness.
motivation: It aims to understand how finite shared randomness and independent classical/quantum interface choices trade off against quantum source cost in correlation generation.
method: The authors formalize a hybrid model with fixed binary projective measurements, fixed classical response functions, and a bounded label budget for shared randomness, then derive tight label bounds and exact minimum source costs for Werner and separable states.
result: Eight labels suffice and the bound is tight; unrestricted labels give zero cost for classically simulable targets and one otherwise; Werner-state costs are exact for every budget, with a visibility jump for three labels; separable states can show nonmonotonic two-label cost.
conclusion: The work provides a distributed-sampling characterization of minimum source cost and worst-case total variation error, clarifying resource tradeoffs in hybrid correlation generation.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper studies a hybrid communication model in which two parties, each holding a prescribed two-qubit quantum source, can independently choose between classical and quantum interfaces. Each party has two fixed binary projective measurements, and the goal is to reproduce the resulting joint outcome distributions exactly for all measurement combinations. The parties share a finite number of classical labels (shared randomness) but do not use the label to coordinate their interface choices; their classical response functions remain fixed across branches. The central question is how many shared labels are needed to achieve a given pair of interface-choice probabilities, and what is the minimum source cost (a measure of quantum resource consumption) for a given label budget. The authors show that eight labels suffice to preserve all feasible pairs of interface-choice probabilities, and this bound is tight. They also recover the known classical four-label bound as a minimum-cost saturation case. With an unrestricted label budget, the minimum source cost is zero if the target distribution can be reproduced by a purely classical protocol, and one otherwise. For Werner states with identical orthogonal measurement pairs, they compute the exact minimum source cost for every label budget: the three-label cost jumps at visibility 2/3, while four labels give zero cost at every visibility. In a family of separable states, the two-label cost varies nonmonotonically with local bias even though the full correlation tensor remains fixed. The analysis is framed as a distributed sampling problem, yielding the minimum source cost at each label budget and the minimum worst-case total variation error for classical protocols with at most two shared labels.
key_contributions: Establishes that eight shared labels are sufficient and necessary to preserve all feasible pairs of interface-choice probabilities in the hybrid model with fixed binary projective measurements.

Derives the exact minimum source cost for Werner states with identical orthogonal measurement pairs as a function of label budget, identifying a sharp transition at visibility 2/3 for three labels and zero cost for four labels at all visibilities.

Shows that in a family of separable states, the two-label cost can vary nonmonotonically with local bias while the full correlation tensor is fixed, highlighting the role of higher-order correlations.
Formulates the problem as a distributed sampling task and determines the minimum worst-case total variation error for classical protocols with at most two shared labels.
Recovers the classical four-label bound as a special case of minimum-cost saturation, connecting the hybrid model to known classical communication complexity results.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors model the hybrid protocol as a distributed sampling problem with shared randomness. Each party's classical response function is fixed across interface choices, and the shared label is not used to coordinate choices, which imposes strong constraints on the achievable joint distributions. The analysis likely employs convex geometry and linear programming to characterize the set of feasible interface-choice probability pairs and to compute the minimum source cost for a given label budget. For Werner states, the symmetry of identical orthogonal measurement pairs allows an exact solution, possibly via semidefinite programming or analytic optimization. The separable-state family is constructed to keep the correlation tensor fixed while varying local bias, enabling a clean demonstration of nonmonotonicity. The worst-case total variation error for classical protocols with limited labels is derived using information-theoretic arguments and combinatorial bounds.
deep_read.results_analysis: The tight eight-label bound is a notable combinatorial result: it shows that no more than eight labels are needed to realize any feasible pair of interface-choice probabilities, and that fewer labels cannot suffice in general. The Werner state analysis yields a precise phase transition: for three labels, the minimum source cost jumps discontinuously at visibility 2/3, indicating a sudden increase in quantum resource requirements. In contrast, four labels achieve zero cost for all visibilities, meaning the quantum source can be entirely replaced by classical communication with four shared labels. The separable-state example reveals that the two-label cost is not monotonic in local bias despite a fixed correlation tensor, underscoring that the cost depends on finer-grained distributional features. The distributed sampling results provide quantitative trade-offs between label budget and total variation error, though specific numerical values for the error bounds are not given in the abstract.
strengths: Provides tight bounds (eight labels) and exact solutions for Werner states, demonstrating a sharp phase transition at visibility 2/3.
Connects the hybrid model to classical communication complexity by recovering the four-label bound and framing the problem as distributed sampling.
Uses a clear and restrictive protocol model (fixed classical responses, no label-based coordination) that yields strong, interpretable results.
Highlights nonmonotonic behavior in separable states, revealing subtleties beyond correlation tensors.
limitations: The analysis is restricted to two fixed binary projective measurements per party and identical orthogonal measurement pairs for Werner states; generalization to more measurements or higher dimensions is not addressed.

The protocol assumes classical response functions are fixed across branches and the shared label is not used to coordinate interface choices, which may limit applicability to more general hybrid scenarios.

Specific numerical values for the worst-case total variation error in the distributed sampling analysis are not provided in the abstract, and the practical implications of the eight-label bound for realistic communication costs are not discussed.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work sits at the intersection of quantum information theory, communication complexity, and resource theories of quantum states. For a researcher interested in quantum physics, it offers a concrete example of how shared randomness can substitute for quantum resources in a distributed setting, with exact trade-off curves for Werner states. The sharp transition at visibility 2/3 is reminiscent of nonlocality thresholds and may inspire further study of resource consumption in hybrid quantum-classical protocols. The distributed sampling perspective connects to broader questions about sampling complexity and the role of correlations in quantum networks.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper presents a rigorous and technically sophisticated analysis of a hybrid quantum-classical model, with tight bounds and exact solutions that reveal nontrivial phenomena such as a discontinuous cost transition and nonmonotonic behavior in separable states. While the model is somewhat stylized, the results are novel and contribute to the understanding of shared randomness as a resource. The connection to classical communication complexity and distributed sampling adds depth. Overall, it is a high-quality theoretical contribution likely to interest specialists in quantum communication and resource theories.

title: All-electronic Geometric Phase Gate On Doppler-cooled Trapped Ions Using An Axial Mode
authors: P. Rahimi, C. Knapp, P. Zantis, T. Maddock, S. J. Hile, J. Randall, M. Siegele-Brown, S. Weidt, W. K. Hensinger
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31534v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report the experimental demonstration of a high-fidelity oscillating magnetic gradient entangling gate on the axial stretch mode of a two-ion crystal in a micro-fabricated surface Paul trap, therefore allowing for mixed-species sympathetic cooling. With only Doppler-cooled [MATH]Yb[MATH] ions at [MATH] = 50(5), we achieve Bell-state fidelities far above the relevant fault-tolerant threshold, simplifying transport protocols within a shuttling-based-architecture. The control fields consist only of an oscillating current applied to submerged integrated wires emitting a B-field gradient near-resonant with the axial mode, and resonant microwave pulses at the qubit frequency constituting very low gate calibration overheads. We also demonstrate an adiabatic elimination of spin-motion entanglement (AESE) version of the gate, showcasing significant robustness.
tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates a high-fidelity all-electronic geometric phase entangling gate on the axial stretch mode of a two-ion crystal in a microfabricated surface Paul trap.
motivation: Trapped-ion quantum computing benefits from simple, low-overhead entangling gates that are compatible with shuttling architectures and mixed-species sympathetic cooling.
method: An oscillating current in submerged integrated wires generates a near-resonant magnetic field gradient, combined with resonant microwave pulses, to drive a geometric phase gate on Doppler-cooled Yb ions; an adiabatic elimination of spin-motion entanglement variant is also demonstrated.

title: Schur Saturation And The Clifford Ceiling In Qudit Css Codes
authors: Jos\'e Alberto Guzm\'an-Vega, Juan Carlos Jim\'enez-Cervantes, Eliseo Sarmiento-Rosales
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Orthogonality-type conditions (triorthogonality in the qubit setting and its prime-dimensional analogues), are the primary algebraic screening criterion for transversal non-Clifford gate constructions in CSS codes. In every known positive construction the certificate is accompanied by a non-Clifford logical gate, leaving open whether a CSS family can satisfy these conditions to arbitrarily high order while admitting no such gate. We answer this question for the class of symmetric spectral CSS codes [MATH] built from character evaluation on a finite abelian group [MATH] with [MATH], [MATH] prime. The mechanism is the identity \[C(A)^\perp * C(A)^\perp=_p^G,\] which we call Schur saturation of the dual code. It follows from the CSS self-orthogonality condition [MATH] and annihilates every local polynomial phase of degree [MATH]. The complete gate-group classification [MATH] shows that every strictly CSS-preserving local-diagonal transversal gate lies at level [MATH] of the Clifford hierarchy, a structural bound we call the Clifford ceiling. The criterion extends to arbitrary CSS pairs satisfying [MATH]; the LDPC instance [MATH] is verified computationally. The false-positive character of the orthogonality certificates is sharpest in the Boolean toric family: these codes satisfy [MATH]-orthogonality for [MATH], yet the non-Clifford sector collapses to zero. The flagship instance [MATH] encodes [MATH] logical ququints at rate [MATH] with distance-[MATH] protection, passes every orthogonality screening test, and yet admits no local-diagonal non-Clifford gate of any degree. The unique non-Pauli survivor is the uniform quadratic drive [MATH], fault-tolerant, logically nontrivial, and Clifford at level [MATH], carrying no magic-state resource.

title: Physical Realization Of The Luczka Model: Inducing Interaction And Entanglement Between Spins
authors: A. R. Kuzmak
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Luczka model describes the interaction of spins with a common bosonic environment in the pure-dephasing regime, in which the bosonic modes couple directly to only one spin component. Due to its specific form of interaction, the model is exactly solvable and has been widely used to describe spin decoherence and effective spin-spin interactions mediated by a common bosonic environment. However, to the best of our knowledge, its physical realization and the specific conditions under which such an interaction can be implemented have not yet been addressed. Here, we propose a physical realization of the Luczka spin-environment interaction by coupling the spin system to unidirectionally propagating, polarized electromagnetic radiation. In contrast to the original Luczka model, which allows an arbitrary angular distribution of photon wave vectors, our scheme gives a unidirectional photon flux with retaining a frequency distribution of the photons. As an illustrative application of the proposed realization, we investigate spin-entanglement dynamics for coherent, single-mode thermal, and Ohmic.

title: From Outcome Exclusion To Measurement Simulation
authors: Kensei Torii, Jiaxi Kuang, Francesco Buscemi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While quantum state exclusion has received considerable attention, the analogous task of measurement outcome exclusion remains less explored. Here we develop a quantitative description of outcome exclusion and extend the resulting framework to obtain necessary and sufficient criteria for measurement simulation by quantum pre-processing and classical post-processing. Our analysis combines two approaches. Algebraic exclusion indices quantify normalized minimum errors in communication tasks with forbidden outputs and yield lower bounds on the number of classical messages required to reproduce the task statistics. Random exclusion profiles provide a statistical description in terms of optimized hypothesis-testing errors and are monotone under both types of processing. This connects outcome exclusion with statistical comparison in the spirit of Blackwell, linking the ability to suppress measurement outcomes to the possibility of simulating one measurement from another.
tldr: The paper develops quantitative measures of measurement outcome exclusion and uses them to characterize when one quantum measurement can be simulated by quantum pre-processing and classical post-processing.
motivation: Quantum state exclusion is well studied, but the dual task of excluding measurement outcomes is less understood; the authors aim to formalize it and connect it to measurement simulation.
method: They introduce algebraic exclusion indices, giving normalized minimum errors and lower bounds on classical message requirements, and random exclusion profiles based on optimized hypothesis-testing errors that are monotone under the allowed processing.
result: The framework yields necessary and sufficient criteria for measurement simulation via quantum pre-processing and classical post-processing, linking outcome exclusion to Blackwell-style statistical comparison.
conclusion: Suppressing forbidden measurement outcomes is quantitatively tied to the possibility of simulating measurements, providing an operational statistical-comparison perspective on quantum measurements.

title: Quantum Control Under Control-Dependent Decoherence
authors: Cyril Morluyan Cordor, Anthony M. Bloch, Eitan Geva
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decoherence, which arises from the interaction of a quantum system with a typically much larger thermal environment, or bath, poses major challenges to the controllability of quantum systems. The dynamics of such open quantum systems is often represented by Markovian quantum master equations of the Lindblad or Redfield type. These equations describe the dynamics of the open system with a sum of coherent (Hamiltonian) and decoherent (dissipative) contributions. It is often assumed that coherent controls only impact the coherent contribution, while the decoherent contribution is taken to be time- and control-independent. However, the decoherent contribution must also be control-dependent if coupling to a thermal bath is to relax the system to a Gibbs state at thermal equilibrium, which is given in terms of the system's Hamiltonian. In this paper, we investigate the effect of accounting for control-dependent decoherence on coherent control protocols. To this end, we examine the effect of accounting for control-dependent decoherence on the controllability of an open quantum system in the case of a two-level system coupled to a thermal bath. We show that coherent controls wield greater influence on the dynamics of the system than predicted by a Lindblad-type equation that models decoherence as time- and control-independent.
tldr: The paper studies how control-dependent decoherence, required for thermodynamic consistency with a thermal bath, changes the controllability of a two-level open quantum system compared with control-independent Lindblad models.
motivation: Standard Lindblad/Redfield master equations often treat decoherence as independent of coherent control, but coupling to a thermal bath should make dissipation control-dependent so that the system relaxes to a Gibbs state determined by the controlled Hamiltonian.
method: The authors analyze a two-level system coupled to a thermal bath and compare control protocols under control-dependent versus control-independent decoherence, focusing on the resulting controllability and influence of coherent controls.
result: They find that coherent controls have a greater influence on the open-system dynamics than predicted by Lindblad-type models with time- and control-independent decoherence.
conclusion: Accounting for control-dependent decoherence is important for accurately assessing quantum controllability and designing coherent control protocols in open quantum systems.

The authors argue that when a two-level system is coupled to a thermal bath, the decoherence rates and Lamb shifts must be control-dependent to ensure relaxation to the correct Gibbs state. They systematically compare the dynamics predicted by a control-independent Lindblad equation with those from a control-dependent master equation derived from a microscopic system-bath model. The central claim is that coherent controls exert a greater influence on the open-system dynamics than the control-independent Lindblad model predicts, implying that controllability is enhanced when control-dependent decoherence is properly accounted for. title: Neural Decoding Of Logical Clifford Circuits With Transversal Gates
authors: Yicheng Guang, Yuliang Xiong, Xun Gao, Yueqi Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On neutral-atom and trapped-ion machines, a transversal gate needs only one syndrome round, so a logical gate takes up to d times less time than with lattice surgery. However, transversal gates make decoding harder, because a transversal CNOT copies errors between two blocks of physical qubits, so a decoder must read all blocks of a circuit together. Algorithmic decoders for such circuits gain accuracy at the cost of speed. Neural decoders ease this trade-off, but they must infer from data where errors go across each gate and how logical outcomes propagate through the circuit, although both are known exactly. In this work, we present Duet, a neural decoder for logical Clifford circuits with transversal gates that builds in this known information and learns only which errors occurred. Duet leverages three insights. First, each transversal gate moves an error to a fixed place, so the network exchanges features only between the sites that a gate connects. Second, a logical outcome propagates through Clifford gates exactly and linearly, so the network predicts only the flips that the errors of each layer cause and combines the layers by a soft XOR. Third, every circuit is built from the same few gates, so the network takes the gates of each layer as input and one network per code distance decodes circuits of different sizes and depths. We pair Duet with the search decoder Tesseract, which re-decodes the few shots on which the network is least confident. On general circuits with 2 to 4 blocks and up to 16 layers, Duet alone is already more accurate than matching at every distance, and with Tesseract it fails 44 times less often than LoMatching at distance 9. On the random circuits of the Lukin group, it fails 0.299 times as often as their neural decoder at distance 7. The composition stays fast and takes 2.4 to 121.7 {\mu}s per layer, less than their network takes per gate at every distance.

motivation: Transversal gates are faster than lattice surgery on neutral-atom and trapped-ion machines but make decoding harder because errors spread across blocks and a decoder must process the full circuit. Existing algorithmic decoders are accurate but slow, while neural decoders trade accuracy for speed without exploiting known circuit structure.
method: Duet builds in the fixed error movement of each transversal gate, uses soft XOR to combine layer-wise predicted logical flips from Clifford propagation, and trains one network per code distance that takes each layer's gates as input. It is paired with the search decoder Tesseract to re-decode the least-confident shots.
result: On general circuits with 2-4 blocks and up to 16 layers, Duet alone outperforms matching at every distance, and with Tesseract it fails 44 times less often than LoMatching at distance 9. On Lukin group random circuits it fails 0.299 times as often as their neural decoder at distance 7, while taking 2.4-121.7 microseconds per layer.
conclusion: The work shows that embedding known circuit-level error and logical propagation structure into neural decoding yields accurate and fast decoding for transversal Clifford circuits, making neural decoders practical for this architecture.

title: Exact Nonstationary Heat-excess Statistics In The Weakly Asymmetric Kipnis--Marchioro--Presutti Model
authors: Baruch Meerson
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact nonstationary large-deviation statistics remain scarce for interacting many-body systems. We find a remarkable nonlocal canonical transformation which maps the weakly asymmetric MFT problem, including its initial and terminal conditions, onto the symmetric problem, previously solved exactly. The resulting rate function is an explicit nonlinear deformation of its symmetric counterpart. We also extend the solution to heat measured beyond an arbitrary observation point.

title: Symmetry-constrained Order Hierarchy Of Connected Optical Responses In A Five-level Rydberg-EIT Medium
authors: Lintian Luo, Weixuan Gu, Yan Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Determining the connected many-body correlations required for a nonlinear optical response of a given order is a central challenge in interacting open quantum systems. We establish a symmetrybased selection rule for connected optical responses in a driven-dissipative Rydberg-EIT model. Under the specified Lindblad conditions, local phase covariance and zero-probe factorization imply that an n-atom connected contribution to the root optical coherence is forbidden below probe-amplitude order 2n-1. Consequently, optical-response coefficients through fifth order involve at most three-atom connected clusters, without assuming weak interatomic interactions. Direct finite-cluster calculations confirm the predicted lowest allowed orders, while an illustrative Maxwell-propagation calculation shows that triplet contributions can partially oppose pair-induced polarization rotation. Our results establish a rigorous connection between optical perturbation order and the connected many-body sectors that can contribute to it.

result: They find that n-atom connected contributions are forbidden below probe-amplitude order 2n−1, so fifth-order response involves at most three-atom clusters; triplet terms can partially oppose pair-induced polarization rotation.
conclusion: The work establishes a rigorous connection between optical perturbation order and allowed connected many-body sectors, showing that symmetry alone imposes a hierarchy on nonlinear optical responses in Rydberg-EIT media.

title: Exact Response Theory Based On Karhunen-Lo\`eve Expansions For Brownian Oscillators
authors: Matteo Colangeli, Lamberto Rondoni, Pasquale Vozza
abstract: ArXiv:2611.32038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend Exact Response Theory (ERT) to an overdamped Brownian oscillator driven by thermal white noise. The stochastic forcing is represented by a Karhunen--Lo\`eve series and embedded into an autonomous, augmented phase space using a harmonic auxiliary phase. This representation allows us to construct the ERT dissipation function for fixed mode amplitudes and recover stochastic averages by averaging over the amplitudes and the initial phase. For the variance, we derive the response at finite spectral truncation and show analytically that, with uniform phase sampling, the full-spectrum white-noise limit reproduces the generator-based result for a sudden temperature change. Furthermore, a comparison with first-order linear response theory highlights how this may fail in general. In particular, if the noise-induced variance is quadratic in the noise amplitude, it is completely omitted by linear response. The analysis provides a framework for this model and for studying more general forcing; extensions to non-Markovian dynamics require separate convergence and regularity analyses.

method: The authors represent thermal white noise as a Karhunen-Loève series, embed it into an augmented autonomous phase space with a harmonic auxiliary phase, and derive the ERT dissipation function for fixed mode amplitudes before averaging over amplitudes and phase.
result: They obtain finite-truncation variance responses and show analytically that, with uniform phase sampling, the full-spectrum white-noise limit reproduces the generator-based result for a sudden temperature change; they also show linear response can fail when noise-induced variance is quadratic in noise amplitude.

title: Exact Approach To Double- And Triple-excitation Bound State In Open Quantum Systems
authors: X. S. Sun, H. T. Cui, Y. A. Yan, H. Z. Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The determination of multiple-excitation bound state in open quantum systems is of broad interest in quantum physics. While the emergence of double- or triple-excitation bound state has been demonstrated in certain specific situations, their universality and exact solvability remain elusive. In this work, we present an exact approach to the double- or triple-excitation dynamics for interacting quantum emitters coupled to environment by deriving a closed equation. By this exact equation, we identify the critical condition for the emergence of double- or triple-excitation bound state, as well as its relationship to the single-excitation one. Our study not only clearly demonstrates the universality of double- or triple-excitation bound state in open quantum emitter systems, but also reveals the possibility of mediating inter-emitter interactions via multiple-excitation bound states.

result: They identify the critical condition for the emergence of double- or triple-excitation bound states, relate these to the single-excitation bound state, and show that such states can mediate inter-emitter interactions.

The authors also discuss the possibility of using these bound states to engineer effective interactions between emitters, which could have implications for quantum simulation and quantum information processing.

title: Quantum State Preparation From Nonreversible Markov Chains Via Spectral Filtering
authors: Wael Drif
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a framework for preparing and transporting coherent quantum samples of nonreversible Markov chains. Our approach uses spectral filtering to construct state-dependent phase operations, which are combined with fixed-point amplitude amplification to transport quantum states along a sequence of related chains. We study two complementary constructions with different oracle requirements and target states. The first uses coherent access to both forward and time-reversed transitions and targets the stationary quantum sample, with a filtering cost governed by a multiplicative-reversibilization gap. The second requires only forward transitions and selects the leading eigenstate of a flat discriminant, which may differ from the stationary quantum sample; we quantify this bias under additional spectral and reversibility-on-average conditions. For the forward-only construction, we implement the spectral filter using generalized quantum signal processing with a single signal qubit, apart from transition registers and oracle workspace. We establish a common transport procedure and derive error and resource bounds that account for spectral properties, overlaps between successive selected states, and the costs of coherent multi-step transition oracles. Up to logarithmic factors, spectral-filter degrees scale inversely with the square roots of the relevant spectral gaps, while transport introduces an additional inverse-square-root dependence on certified lower bounds on squared overlaps between successive selected states. Our results extend existing nonreversible spectral methods to multistage coherent state transport with controlled approximation errors.
tldr: A framework using spectral filtering and fixed-point amplitude amplification to coherently prepare and transport quantum samples of nonreversible Markov chains.
motivation: Nonreversible Markov chains offer faster mixing but lack the symmetric/detailed-balance structure exploited by standard quantum walk-based sampling algorithms, so coherent sample preparation for them is underdeveloped.
method: Two constructions are given: one with coherent access to forward and time-reversed transitions targeting the stationary quantum sample, and one using only forward transitions with generalized quantum signal processing to filter a flat discriminant's leading eigenstate; a shared transport procedure chains filtered states across related chains.
result: Error and resource bounds show filter degree scaling as the inverse square root of relevant spectral gaps, with transport adding an inverse-square-root dependence on certified lower bounds of squared overlaps between successive states; bias of the forward-only construction is quantified under spectral and average-reversibility conditions.
conclusion: The work extends nonreversible spectral methods to multistage coherent state transport with controlled approximation error, at costs governed by reversibilization-like gaps and inter-stage overlaps.

title: Geometric Control Of Electronic Decoherence In A Chiral Spin-Orbit Coupled Helix
authors: Neel Moudgal, Nicholas A. Kotov, Eitan Geva
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While chirality is known to impact chemical and optical properties of molecular systems, as well as their biological function, far less is known about its impact on quantum coherence. By considering a chiral helix as a paradigmatic model, we show that within the Born-Markov regime, changing the degree of helical twist can be used to modulate the electronic decoherence rate. Moderate to strong spin-orbit coupling between next-nearest-neighbor sites along the helix are shown to give rise to a strong dependence of the electronic decoherence rate on the degree of chirality. The effect of chirality on electronic decoherence rates is also seen to be strongly impacted by the spatial and temporal correlations between the local environmental fluctuations to which the local excitations along the helix are subject. Our results show that chirality can serve as a tunable design parameter for quantum engineering and highlight the importance role environmental correlations can play in determining how chirality affects electronic decoherence rates.
tldr: The paper shows that the helical twist angle in a chiral spin-orbit-coupled helix can tune electronic decoherence rates within the Born-Markov regime, with strong dependence on environmental correlation properties.
motivation: Chirality is known to affect chemical, optical, and biological properties, but its impact on quantum coherence and decoherence remains poorly understood.
method: The authors model a chiral helix with next-nearest-neighbor spin-orbit coupling and analyze electronic decoherence using a Born-Markov open quantum system framework, varying helical twist and environmental spatial/temporal correlations.
result: Moderate to strong spin-orbit coupling produces a strong dependence of the electronic decoherence rate on chirality, and the effect is strongly modulated by spatial and temporal correlations of local environmental fluctuations.
conclusion: Chirality can serve as a tunable design parameter for quantum engineering, and environmental correlations play an important role in how chirality affects electronic decoherence.

title: Eliminating Incompatibility In Quantum Multiparameter Estimation With Antiparallel Probes
authors: Souradeep Sasmal, Bakmou Lahcen, Kok Chuan Tan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.32036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters is fundamentally constrained by complementarity and measurement incompatibility, which limits the sensitivity of quantum measurement devices by preventing the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) Cram\'er-Rao bound (CRB) from being saturated. We show that antiparallel probe configurations can overcome this limitation when the dynamics of the parameter encoding preserve the said configurations. We characterise the quantum channels that satisfy this requirement and establish conditions under which such configurations exist and can saturate the SLD-CRB without compromising the quantum Fisher information, leading to a metrological advantage. For qubit probes, we prove that this advantage is present if and only if the encoding channel is unital. We extend this analysis to the two probe, finite dimensional qudit case by considering derivative reversal and transpose map based probe states, as well as more general multiprobe configurations. For each of these cases, we identify conditions under which an advantage exists. Our results establish connections between channel symmetries, probe configurations and the attainability of multiparameter precision limits.
tldr: The paper shows that antiparallel probe configurations can eliminate measurement incompatibility in quantum multiparameter estimation and saturate the SLD Cramér-Rao bound under suitable encoding channels.
motivation: Simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters is limited by complementarity and measurement incompatibility, which prevents saturating the SLD-Cramér-Rao bound and thus restricts quantum metrological sensitivity.
method: The authors characterize quantum channels that preserve antiparallel probe configurations, establish conditions for saturating the SLD-CRB without reducing quantum Fisher information, and analyze qubit and finite-dimensional qudit cases using derivative reversal and transpose-map-based probe states.
result: For qubit probes, the metrological advantage exists if and only if the encoding channel is unital; extensions to two-probe qudits and general multiprobe configurations identify further conditions for advantage.
conclusion: The work links channel symmetries, probe configurations, and attainability of multiparameter precision limits, providing a route to overcome incompatibility in quantum estimation.

title: Internal Inconsistencies And Unresolved Experimental Evidence In A Quantum Neurosecurity Framework
authors: S. Grigorovich, M. Bairachnaya, E. Daroczi, J. Marshall, B. Giros
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article presents a technical and theoretical assessment of the Quantum-Entangled Neuro-Symbolic Swarm Federation (QENSSF), a framework intended for privacy-preserving, quantum-secure, AI-powered, multimodal healthcare data analysis, introduced by Ben Othman and Ali (2025). They claim QENSSF is a first-in-class framework with provable privacy and security guarantees, support these with theorems and proofs, report an experimental evaluation on IBM's quantum Eagle processor, report a real-world quantum key distribution (QKD) test, and claim use of real-world multimodal datasets (ADNI, UK Biobank, and MIMIC-IV). Our examination of quantitative support for these claims identified various concerns. Most importantly, the security criterion of a central guarantee (Theorem 1) cannot be satisfied given the risk formulation and relevant constraints, which, along with calculation errors in the proof, directly undermines the claim of provable security. Furthermore, insufficient reporting of biomedical datasets and unresolved discrepancies in the hardware evaluation limit verification of the experimental claims and overall reproducibility. QENSSF identifies a real need: ensuring privacy and security of healthcare data while patients benefit from AI-powered analysis. This need is particularly pressing for sensitive neural data, including the neuroimaging data available through sources such as ADNI. Privacy concerns also extend to wearable EEG data, for which reidentification risks can persist despite deidentification. However, QENSSF's foundational inconsistencies need resolution before it could be considered in the neurosecurity domain.
tldr: A technical critique identifies internal inconsistencies and unresolved experimental discrepancies in the QENSSF quantum neurosecurity framework, undermining its claimed provable security.
motivation: The paper assesses a proposed privacy-preserving, quantum-secure AI framework for healthcare data and tests whether its security theorems and experimental claims are valid and reproducible.
method: The authors examine the quantitative support for QENSSF's security proof, including Theorem 1, and review the reported IBM Eagle processor evaluation, QKD test, and use of biomedical datasets.
result: They find that Theorem 1's security criterion cannot be satisfied under the stated risk formulation, that the proof contains calculation errors, and that dataset reporting and hardware evaluation discrepancies prevent verification.
conclusion: The QENSSF framework addresses a real need for secure healthcare data analysis, but its foundational inconsistencies must be resolved before it can be considered in the neurosecurity domain.

title: A Counterexample To The Ho-Hsieh Vqcs Saturation Conjecture
authors: Edward Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that there exists a 4-qubit state that can be prepared by a variational quantum-classical simulation (VQCS) circuit ansatz containing 3 layers, but not with 2 layers. This disproves the strong form of a conjecture presented by Ho and Hsieh stating that the expressivity of VQCS on [MATH] qubits saturates at [MATH] layers. The weak form of the conjecture concerning the preparation of the ground state remains open.
tldr: The paper disproves the strong form of the Ho-Hsieh conjecture by constructing a 4-qubit state preparable with a 3-layer VQCS ansatz but not with 2 layers.
motivation: Ho and Hsieh conjectured that the expressivity of variational quantum-classical simulation circuits on M qubits saturates at M layers; this work tests and refutes the strong form of that conjecture.
method: The author explicitly constructs a 4-qubit state and analyzes the capabilities of VQCS circuit ansatze with 2 versus 3 layers to show a separation in state-preparation power.
result: A 4-qubit state is shown to be preparable by a 3-layer VQCS circuit but not by any 2-layer VQCS circuit, providing a counterexample to the saturation conjecture.
conclusion: The strong form of the Ho-Hsieh VQCS saturation conjecture is false, while the weak form concerning ground-state preparation remains open.

title: Variance And Higher-Order Moments In Computational Fluctuating Hydrodynamics With Multiplicative Noise
authors: Satinderpreet Singh, Changho Kim, Ishan Srivastava, Andrew J. Nonaka, John B. Bell, Alejandro L. Garcia
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fluctuating hydrodynamics (FHD) models mesoscopic fluid systems by augmenting classical conservation laws with stochastic flux terms governed by the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. While traditional validation of computational FHD (CFHD) algorithms focuses primarily on second-order central moments of equilibrium fluctuations, accurately resolving higher-order moments, such as skewness and kurtosis, is essential for evaluating non-linear functions of hydrodynamic fields. In this work, we analyze finite-volume CFHD discretizations to evaluate second-, third-, and fourth-order central moments of thermodynamic fluctuations. Using the one-dimensional stochastic heat equation, we demonstrate that incorporating multiplicative noise is necessary to recover the expected gamma distribution for temperature in the canonical ensemble, whereas additive noise models yield a Gaussian distribution that fails to capture non-zero skewness and excess kurtosis. We also derive analytical expressions for inherent modeling errors that persist in the limit of vanishing time step for a variety of boundary conditions. Furthermore, we introduce an improved formulation for Dirichlet boundary conditions that eliminates large boundary-adjacent errors in the third central moment present in traditional boundary treatments. We also examine higher-order temporal integration schemes, demonstrating that Stratonovich-based integrators, such as Heun's predictor-corrector method, can reduce these modeling errors. Finally, numerical simulations of the full compressible, stochastic Navier--Stokes equations confirm the generality and practical applicability of the findings obtained from the stochastic heat equation.
tldr: The paper analyzes finite-volume discretizations of computational fluctuating hydrodynamics, showing that multiplicative noise is needed to recover higher-order thermodynamic fluctuation moments and deriving error expressions for stochastic heat equation discretizations.
motivation: Standard validation of computational fluctuating hydrodynamics focuses on second-order moments, but higher-order moments such as skewness and kurtosis are important for nonlinear functions of hydrodynamic fields and for correctly capturing non-Gaussian equilibrium fluctuations.
method: The authors study one-dimensional stochastic heat equation discretizations with additive versus multiplicative noise, derive analytical modeling errors for various boundary conditions and time integrators, and validate findings with full compressible stochastic Navier-Stokes simulations.
result: Multiplicative noise recovers the expected gamma distribution for temperature and captures nonzero skewness and excess kurtosis, while additive noise yields an incorrect Gaussian distribution; improved Dirichlet boundary treatment and Stratonovich-type integrators reduce modeling errors.
conclusion: Accurate higher-order fluctuation statistics in computational fluctuating hydrodynamics require multiplicative noise and careful numerical treatment, with implications for mesoscopic fluid simulation validation.

title: Ground-State Chiral Quantum Clusters
authors: Adolfo Del Campo Matteo Massaro
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31370v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum time crystals are states of matter that spontaneously break time translation symmetry, extending the notion of crystalline order to time. While their out-of-equilibrium version has been successfully realized by periodic driving, the equilibrium counterpart remains elusive. Here we introduce "ground-state chiral quantum clusters": self-bound many-body ground states supporting a persistent current. We provide a minimal field theory describing these states, and an exact microscopic realization via the attractive anyonic Lieb-Liniger model on a ring. In the latter, the ground-state density-density correlator exhibits the Talbot effect, with a soliton-like profile that periodically disperses and revives while drifting indefinitely along the ring, realizing persistent motion at equilibrium. Possible experimental probes are discussed.
tldr: The authors introduce 'ground-state chiral quantum clusters' — self-bound equilibrium many-body ground states carrying persistent currents — and realize them exactly in the attractive anyonic Lieb-Liniger model on a ring.
motivation: Quantum time crystals, which spontaneously break time-translation symmetry, have been realized only in periodically driven out-of-equilibrium settings; an equilibrium counterpart remains elusive and motivates the search for ground states with persistent motion.
method: A minimal field theory for these states is constructed, together with an exact microscopic solution of the attractive anyonic Lieb-Liniger model on a ring, whose ground-state density-density correlator is analyzed and shown to exhibit a Talbot-like soliton profile.
result: The ground state displays a soliton-like density profile that periodically disperses and revives while drifting indefinitely along the ring, yielding persistent motion at equilibrium; possible experimental probes are discussed.
conclusion: Equilibrium persistent currents may be realizable in anyonic/attractive one-dimensional ring systems, offering a candidate equilibrium analogue of time-crystalline order.

title: How Small Can A Single Shor Run Be? Limits And Constructions For Secp256k1
authors: Yicheng Guang, Yuliang Xiong, Yueqi Chen, Xun Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most resource estimates for breaking secp256k1 with Shor's algorithm describe one long run per attempt, and the spacetime volume of that run, its peak number of logical qubits times its Toffoli count, sets its logical-error budget. Eker{\aa}'s tradeoff shrinks each run by using more runs, but how far it can shrink the largest run, and at what circuit cost, has not been determined. We minimize the volume of the largest run while every key is recovered with probability at least 0.99, within ten times the total volume of three runs of H\"aner et al.\ and [MATH] classical operations. We prove that a linear run fixed in advance, which starts its group register at a point and discards its label, reveals at most [MATH] bits about a uniform key, where [MATH] counts its exponent values and [MATH] is the group order. With generic post-processing and the baseline's window costs, splitting alone then shrinks the largest run at most 1.86 times within the budget. To gain more, we make each exponent bit cheaper with windows that share one table point among exponent values related by six symmetries of the curve, on a point-addition core borrowed from the ECDSA.Fail leaderboard. One random scalar and one random start per run give every approximate addition uniform operands, and a bound on each run's outcomes certifies, for every key, a decoder that discards flagged runs. We count every Toffoli gate and every qubit of every run, and each configuration solved all 563 of its pre-registered simulated trials on secp256k1. The best one shrinks the largest run 3.87 times at 8.79 times the baseline's total volume, against 2.81 times for Eker{\aa}'s tradeoff on the same core, and its run is at least 2.6 times smaller than every design of Initio Intelligence.
tldr: The paper determines how small the largest single Shor run against secp256k1 can be made by trading run size against the number of runs and circuit cost, achieving a 3.87x reduction in the largest run at 8.79x the baseline spacetime volume.
motivation: Prior resource estimates for breaking secp256k1 assume one long Shor run, and while Ekerå's tradeoff reduces run size using more runs, the limits of that shrinking and its circuit cost were unknown.
method: The authors bound the information revealed by a fixed linear run, analyze splitting with generic post-processing, then reduce per-bit exponent cost using windowed exponentiation sharing table points via six curve symmetries on an ECDSA.Fail point-addition core, counting all Toffolis and qubits and validating on 563 pre-registered simulated trials.
result: Splitting alone shrinks the largest run at most 1.86x within the budget, while the optimized construction shrinks it 3.87x at 8.79x the baseline total volume, better than Ekerå's 2.81x and at least 2.6x smaller than Initio Intelligence designs.
conclusion: Practical limits on single-run Shor executions for secp256k1 are established, showing that meaningful reductions in peak logical qubit count are possible only at substantial total spacetime cost.

title: A Machine Learning Architecture For Scaling Of Holographic Quantum Circuits
authors: Michael L. Wall Cliff Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We describe an architecture and workflow for learning and generalizing the syntax and parameters of holographic quantum circuits (HQCs), which are natural quantum circuit analogs of classical tensor networks. An HQC uses mid-circuit measurements and resets on a small subset of "physical" qubits whose measurement outcomes become correlated through coupling with a register of persistent "ancilla" qubits, analogous to the physical and bond indices of a tensor network. Hence, an HQC with fixed qubit resources can efficiently generate samples from a large quantum state, and adding qubits to the HQC ansatz has the effect of exponentially increasing the effective bond dimension. Our machine learning approach provides mechanisms for harnessing both features of HQCs by extrapolating the syntax (e.g., a sequence of gates, measurements, and resets) and parameters (e.g., the angles appearing in single-qubit rotations) from a dataset of HQCs to longer or more expressive HQCs. We demonstrate the methodology and its performance on an analytically solvable dataset formed by a vector-valued generalization of the W-state. Finally, we provide an outlook for usage of the methodology for scaling the effective bond dimensions of HQCs in quantum simulation.
tldr: The paper proposes a machine-learning workflow to learn and extrapolate the syntax and parameters of holographic quantum circuits, which mimic tensor networks via mid-circuit measurements and ancilla qubits.
motivation: Holographic quantum circuits can efficiently represent large quantum states with limited physical qubits, but scaling their structure and parameters to larger effective bond dimensions is challenging.
method: The authors develop an architecture that learns gate/measurement/reset sequences and rotation angles from a dataset of HQCs, then extrapolates to longer or more expressive circuits, demonstrated on an analytically solvable vector-valued W-state dataset.
result: The methodology successfully generalizes HQC syntax and parameters to scaled circuits on the synthetic dataset, showing potential for increasing effective bond dimension.
conclusion: The approach offers a route to automate scaling of HQCs for quantum simulation, though validation on physically relevant non-analytic problems remains future work.

title: Apqke-dr: Entropy-Failure Analysis Of A Post-Quantum-Initialized Ratcheted Channel
authors: Muhammad Asfand Hafeez, Zain Ul Abideen, Amna Zafar, Kazi Hassan Shakib, Arslan Munir
abstract: ArXiv:2611.32024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-lived secure channels for embedded and cyber-physical systems (CPSs) must resist quantum attacks and failures in endpoint randomness. While several post-quantum key exchange protocols exist, their security assumes reliable randomness at the endpoint, but this assumption is not always true in embedded devices. In this paper, we introduce the Entropy Attack Suite (EAS) to evaluate secure channels facing endpoint randomness failures, such as low-entropy boot and Random Number Generation (RNG) path subversion. As a case study, we design and implement APQKE-DR, a post-quantum secure channel. Its handshake uses ML-KEM [1] and ML-DSA [2], producing a root key for an X25519 Double Ratchet. We assess the performance of APQKE-DR and security for smart grid communication, and integrate it beneath ANSI C12.22 and DNP3 without altering payload formats. On a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5, the APQKE handshake exchanges 9,610 bytes with median latencies of 1.99 ms (node) and 0.82 ms (server). The ratcheted channel adds 31 bytes per message. With fresh randomness and ideal cryptographic primitives, ProVerif verifies the modeled secrecy and authentication properties. If randomness fails, EAS can recover the RNG stream and root key from public transcripts. Under RNG-path subversion, a weak generator exposes the root key across sessions. If subversion also affects X25519 keys, attackers may access ratchet keys and plaintexts. TPM seeding prevents early-boot attacks but not later subversion, while measured boot can block modified firmware. Secure deployment thus requires integrity along the entire entropy path, not just strong cryptographic primitives.
tldr: The authors build APQKE-DR, a hybrid post-quantum handshake (ML-KEM + ML-DSA) feeding an X25519 Double Ratchet, and use an 'Entropy Attack Suite' to show that failures in endpoint randomness can leak the root key and plaintexts.
motivation: Long-lived secure channels in embedded and cyber-physical systems (e.g., smart grids) need resistance to quantum attacks, but existing post-quantum key exchange protocols assume reliable endpoint randomness, an assumption that often fails in low-cost embedded devices.
method: They design and implement APQKE-DR beneath ANSI C12.22 and DNP3 without changing payload formats, benchmark it on a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5, verify modeled secrecy and authentication with ProVerif under ideal randomness, and then apply an entropy attack suite simulating low-entropy boot and RNG-path subversion.
result: The handshake exchanges 9,610 bytes with median latencies of 1.99 ms (node) and 0.82 ms (server), adding 31 bytes per ratcheted message; when randomness fails, attackers can recover the RNG stream and root key from public transcripts, and with X25519 key subversion may reach ratchet keys and plaintexts, while TPM seeding only blocks early-boot attacks and measured boot blocks modified firmware.
conclusion: Secure deployment requires integrity along the entire entropy path, not merely strong post-quantum cryptographic primitives, and practical protocols must be hardened against endpoint randomness failures.

title: Low-Degree Torus Approximations Of The And Function And $\mathsf{ACC}^0$ Circuits
authors: Ryuhei Mori Shuhei Osaki
abstract: ArXiv:2611.32163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Torus polynomials, real polynomials evaluated modulo one, were proposed by Bhrushundi, Hosseini, Lovett, and Rao as a route to [MATH] lower bounds. We prove degree upper bounds for torus polynomials approximating a function on every input. First, for every [MATH], [MATH] has an [MATH]-approximating torus polynomial of degree [MATH], improving the previous [MATH]. This is optimal up to constant factors for inverse-polynomial error, by a lower bound of Krishan and Vishwanathan, and refutes two superlogarithmic-degree conjectures of Krishan and Sarma. Second, for every Boolean function [MATH] computed by a depth-[MATH], size-[MATH] [MATH] circuit, [MATH] has an [MATH]-approximating torus polynomial of degree at most [MATH], where [MATH] is the number of distinct prime factors of [MATH] and [MATH] depends only on [MATH]. This improves the bound [MATH] of Bhrushundi, Hosseini, Lovett, and Rao, making the exponent of [MATH] linear in the depth and the dependence on [MATH] linear. Both proofs sample terms of a Fourier expansion and approximate them by low-degree torus polynomials. A torus approximation of degree [MATH] can be written as a linear combination of at most [MATH] parities, called a periodic Fourier representation, which is known to give a non-adaptive measurement-based quantum computation with linear side-processing using one qubit per parity. Hence every [MATH] function can be computed with quasipolynomially many qubits and inverse-polynomial error probability on every input. Conversely, we prove that a periodic Fourier representation with [MATH] parities and error probability [MATH] gives a torus approximation of degree [MATH], so the two notions are equivalent.
tldr: The paper proves improved degree upper bounds for torus polynomial approximations to the AND function and to Boolean functions computed by ACC^0 circuits, with an equivalence to periodic Fourier representations and implications for measurement-based quantum computation.
motivation: Torus polynomials were proposed as a route to ACC^0 lower bounds, and the authors aim to sharpen known degree bounds and resolve conjectures about superlogarithmic-degree approximations.
method: The proofs sample terms of Fourier expansions and approximate them by low-degree torus polynomials; the paper also establishes an equivalence between torus approximations and periodic Fourier representations.
result: The authors obtain an optimal-up-to-constants degree bound for AND, improve the ACC^0 degree bound to depend linearly on depth and on the number of distinct prime factors, and show that every ACC^0 function can be computed with quasipolynomially many qubits in a non-adaptive MBQC model.
conclusion: The work advances classical circuit complexity and clarifies the connection between torus approximations and periodic Fourier representations, with a secondary implication for measurement-based quantum computation.

title: Blueprint For Doe Quantum Supercomputing
authors: Ryan Bennink, Robin Blume-Kohout, Salman Habib, Andrew Landahl, Hai Ah Nam, Laura Schulz, Mallikarjun Shankar, Nicholas Wright
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computing stands at the threshold of a transformative decade, where the field will evolve from small-scale demonstrations toward practical scientific computing at scale. This Blueprint identifies fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs) as a viable, scalable, and broadly applicable path to achieving "quantum scientific utility." It outlines a strategy to prepare the US Department of Energy (DOE) for FTQCs and their integration into the US national scientific computing infrastructure. Its purpose is to identify the steps, milestones, and research directions necessary for DOE to enable initial deployment of FTQCs in 2028 as a scientific tool for the nation and mature this capability into the 2030s. Given recent demonstrations of logical operations on error-corrected logical qubits and the advancement of commercial hardware roadmaps, DOE should begin preparations for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing deployment for DOE science missions. This Blueprint proposes that DOE focus on (1) deploying first-generation scientifically relevant quantum computers with at least 100 logical qubits and performing at least 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations in scientifically relevant calculations; (2) developing essential FTQC programming competencies, system software, and facility readiness; and (3) investing in cutting-edge focused R&D that fosters breakthroughs in scientific applications, algorithms, and logical architectures needed to accelerate the advent of scientific utility. This effort will position DOE to transition to larger systems: production-scale quantum computers that comprise 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits, perform 1 to 10 billion hard logical operations, and execute scientifically useful computations at scale. The Blueprint calls for transformative R&D and collective action to accelerate the advent of scientific quantum utility and bring it within reach by 2028.
tldr: A DOE strategic blueprint outlining milestones and R&D priorities for deploying fault-tolerant quantum computers with 100+ logical qubits as scientific instruments by 2028.
motivation: Recent demonstrations of logical operations on error-corrected qubits and commercial hardware roadmaps suggest fault-tolerant quantum computing is approaching scientific utility, prompting the US Department of Energy to plan its integration into national scientific computing infrastructure.
method: Programmatic roadmap and gap analysis: identifies target metrics (100 logical qubits, 10^4-10^5 logical operations for first-generation systems; 10^3-10^4 logical qubits and 10^9-10^10 operations for production scale), and lays out needs in programming competency, system software, facility readiness, and focused R&D on applications, algorithms, and logical architectures.
result: No new technical results; the document proposes a deployment timeline targeting initial FTQC deployment in 2028 and maturation through the 2030s, with recommendations for DOE investment and collective action.
conclusion: The blueprint argues that coordinated R&D and infrastructure investment can bring quantum scientific utility within reach by 2028, but it is a policy/strategy document rather than a technical contribution.

title: High Throughput Meets Low Latency: Ckks Functional Bootstrapping On GPUs
authors: Carlos Agull\'o-Domingo, Carlo Pascoe, \'oscar Vera-L\'opez, Andreea Alexandru, Ahmad Al Badawi, Jos\'e L. Abell\'an, Yuriy Polyakov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Functional (programmable) bootstrapping extends the bootstrapping operation of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to evaluate an arbitrary function while refreshing a ciphertext. This capability was a unique feature of scalar CGGI/DM cryptosystems for many years until it was recently added to the toolset of vectorized FHE schemes, with CKKS being the most promising option both in terms of throughput (amortized time) and functionality. Previous work showed that CKKS functional bootstrapping outperforms CGGI/DM functional bootstrapping in terms of throughput by two to three orders of magnitude, but still loses in latency on CPU by two to three orders of magnitude. We present an optimized GPU implementation of CKKS functional bootstrapping that closes the latency gap. Our implementation supports evaluating functions over both small integers (as in CGGI/DM) and real numbers (unique to CKKS), which we call discrete-CKKS and continuous-CKKS functional bootstrapping, respectively.
tldr: A GPU-accelerated implementation of CKKS functional bootstrapping that closes the latency gap with scalar CGGI/DM schemes while retaining high throughput.
motivation: Functional bootstrapping in vectorized FHE schemes such as CKKS offers orders-of-magnitude better throughput than CGGI/DM but suffers from two to three orders of magnitude worse latency on CPUs; the authors aim to eliminate this latency disadvantage.
method: The authors design and optimize a GPU implementation of CKKS functional bootstrapping, supporting both discrete-CKKS (small integers, as in CGGI/DM) and continuous-CKKS (real-valued functions) evaluation modes.
result: The GPU implementation substantially reduces latency compared to prior CPU-based CKKS functional bootstrapping, closing the gap with CGGI/DM while preserving the throughput advantage of the vectorized scheme.
conclusion: GPU acceleration makes CKKS functional bootstrapping competitive in latency as well as throughput, broadening the practicality of programmable FHE for real-valued function evaluation.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Two Source Extractors For Arbitrary Constant Entropy Rate
authors: Xin Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.32086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct explicit two-source extractors for any constant entropy rate with asymptotically optimal parameters. Specifically, for sources on [MATH] bits with min-entropy [MATH] for any constant [MATH], and error [MATH] where [MATH] is a constant depending on [MATH], our extractor outputs [MATH] bits that are [MATH] close to uniform. In particular, this gives two-source extractors with [MATH] output bits and [MATH] error for any constant entropy rate. Previously, explicit two source extractors with such error are only known to work for entropy rate roughly [MATH] (Bourgain 2005, Lewko 2019). We also extend our constructions to give (strong) non-malleable two source extractors and sumset extractors for any constant entropy rate with asymptotically optimal parameters. Our extractors can be extended to handle slightly sub-constant entropy rate, with sub-optimal error. Using a different construction and analysis, we give explicit (non-malleable) two source extractors for entropy [MATH] for some constant [MATH] with [MATH] output bits and error close to [MATH]. An independent work of Doron and Goodman constructed explicit two-source extractors for entropy [MATH] with error [MATH] for some constant [MATH]. Their extractors work for smaller entropy than ours, while our extractors have better error and output length for any constant entropy rate. Our extractors for entropy [MATH] are obtained independently before we were aware of their results, while our extractors for constant entropy rate with asymptotically optimal parameters are obtained after we learned their unpublished results at the Simons Institute, using different ideas and techniques.
tldr: The paper constructs explicit classical two-source extractors for arbitrary constant entropy rate with asymptotically optimal output length and error.
motivation: Two-source extractors are fundamental pseudorandomness objects, but prior explicit constructions with optimal error were limited to entropy rates around 1/2; this work aims to achieve optimal parameters for any constant entropy rate.
method: The author gives new explicit constructions and analyses for two-source extractors, extending them to strong non-malleable two-source extractors and sumset extractors, and also handles slightly sub-constant entropy rate with sub-optimal error.
result: For any constant entropy rate, the extractors output a constant fraction of the entropy and achieve error exponentially small in the output length, improving over previous work and matching independent work by Doron and Goodman in different parameter regimes.
conclusion: The paper resolves a central open problem in classical randomness extraction, but the results are entirely classical and do not directly address quantum information-theoretic questions.

title: Beyond Classical Minimax Rates: Quantum Sampling In Gradient-Based Simulation Optimization
authors: Hao Cao, Jian-Qiang Hu, Mingjie Hu, Qixin Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.32004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study gradient-based search for a class of convex simulation optimization problems with gradients estimated from noisy outputs.
