The associated traveling wave equations are solutions of four-dimensional dynamical systems, leading to both computational challenges and rich structural behavior. In particular, to describe the properties of these traveling waves, we analyze heteroclinic orbits that connect two distinct equilibria, one of which undergoes a transition in the four-dimensional phase space from a saddle-focus to a saddle point as the dissipation parameter increases. This transition governs the nature of the wave profile, which evolves smoothly from an oscillatory shock wave to a regularized (non-oscillatory) shock wave. To compute such solutions, we introduce a finite-difference-based numerical method tailored for this class of problems.
tldr: The paper analyzes heteroclinic orbits in a four-dimensional dynamical system governing traveling-wave solutions of dissipative Bona-Smith/Boussinesq water-wave models, showing a saddle-focus to saddle transition that changes wave profiles from oscillatory to regularized shocks.
motivation: Oscillatory and regularized shock waves (undular bores) in shallow water arise from the interplay of dispersion, nonlinearity and dissipation, and their structure is not fully understood for dissipative Boussinesq-type models.
method: Traveling-wave ansatz reduces the Bona-Smith systems to a four-dimensional autonomous ODE system; the authors study heteroclinic connections between two equilibria and develop a tailored finite-difference numerical scheme to compute these orbits.
result: As the dissipation parameter increases, one equilibrium changes from saddle-focus to saddle, and correspondingly the computed wave profiles transition smoothly from oscillatory shock waves to non-oscillatory regularized shocks.
conclusion: The saddle-focus to saddle transition in the 4D phase space organizes the qualitative shape of dissipative Boussinesq traveling waves, and the proposed numerical method reliably captures such heteroclinic solutions.

title: Spontaneous Synchronization In Cellular Circadian Clocks
authors: Yuelong Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a population of identical cellular circadian oscillators, each a four-species transcription--translation feedback loop of the type analysed by Wang and Peskin, coupled by the exchange of cytoplasmic mRNA with a shared, well-mixed bloodstream at rate [MATH]. Simulations started from uniformly random phases show a collective damping of the mean rhythm followed by spontaneous synchronization. We show that the blood compartment tracks the population mean on the time scale [MATH], and that the population means obey the single-cell equations with a correction proportional to the variance [MATH] of nuclear protein across cells; the correction is accurate only near synchrony. Deviations from the mean obey a linear system with periodic coefficients, whose leading Floquet exponent [MATH] is the asymptotic synchronization rate. Using the fact that the four first-order stages of the feedback loop commute, we prove that [MATH] on the limit cycle in the large-population limit. Numerically computed exponents agree with the decay rates measured in simulations to within [MATH] for [MATH] to [MATH] cells. The approach to synchrony from an incoherent state is slower than [MATH], and at the weakest coupling tested the population remains in a two-cluster state. With intrinsic molecular noise, uncoupled cells lose their autocorrelation within about ten cycles, whereas coupled cells retain it and sustain a Kuramoto order parameter of [MATH] to [MATH].
tldr: The paper models a population of coupled cellular circadian oscillators and analyzes spontaneous synchronization via mean-field coupling and Floquet exponents.
motivation: To understand how identical cellular circadian clocks synchronize through exchange of mRNA with a shared blood compartment, and to characterize the synchronization dynamics analytically.
method: A four-species transcription-translation feedback loop model is coupled through a well-mixed blood compartment; the authors derive mean-field equations, a linearized periodic-coefficient system, and compute the leading Floquet exponent as the synchronization rate, supported by numerical simulations.
result: The blood compartment tracks the population mean, and the leading Floquet exponent is proven on the limit cycle in the large-population limit; simulations confirm agreement with measured decay rates, with slow approach to synchrony and noise-induced sustained oscillations.
conclusion: The study provides a quantitative theory of synchronization in coupled circadian clocks, showing that coupling via a shared compartment can overcome molecular noise and maintain collective rhythmicity.

title: The Industrialization Of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving Is The Same Old Dead End
authors: Richard Lipton Richard Demillo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nearly fifty years ago, DeMillo, Lipton, and Perlis argued that mathematical proofs are not static, isolated structures of formal logic, but the products of a vibrant, evolving social process of human critique, internalization, and shared intuition. In October 2026, OpenAI challenged this thesis by releasing a massive repository of 722 automated mathematical manuscripts, claiming full or partial solutions to 372 longstanding open problems. This paper examines the immediate crisis through the lens of the original DLP framework. We argue that the sudden, automated overproduction of dense, unreadable proofs represents an industrial pollution of the mathematical ecosystem. By examining the three fatal structural pillars of this automated approach (Specification, Regress, and Utility), we demonstrate that decoupling the act of mechanical solving from the human social process of understanding produces a sterile repository of dead logical artifacts. The resulting industrialization of unexamined manuscripts is self-fulfilling. Flooding the literature guarantees that the finite supply of human attention will lose the race to separate signal from noise. In this sense, posting a result is not the same act as submitting it to the community processes by which mathematics is vetted, digested, and incorporated into shared knowledge.
tldr: The paper argues that automated mathematical proof generation, exemplified by OpenAI's 2026 release of 722 manuscripts, produces an industrial flood of unreadable proofs that bypasses the social process required for mathematical understanding.
motivation: It revisits the DeMillo-Lipton-Perlis thesis that proofs are socially embedded and uses it to critique the recent surge of AI-generated mathematical manuscripts claiming solutions to open problems.
method: The authors analyze the automated proof-solving phenomenon through the DLP framework, identifying three structural failures: Specification, Regress, and Utility, and arguing that mechanical solving is decoupled from human comprehension.
result: They conclude that automated overproduction pollutes the mathematical ecosystem, as the finite supply of human attention cannot keep up with the volume of unvetted manuscripts, making posting a result fundamentally different from community validation.
conclusion: The industrialization of unexamined proofs is a dead end because mathematical knowledge requires social vetting, internalization, and shared intuition, not merely mechanical solution generation.

title: Towards Efficient Attack Tree Generation From Attack Graphs For Unobservable Target Analysis
authors: Chijioke Eze, Aliyu Tanko Ali, Leonard Chidiebere Eze, Antonello Monti, Damas Gruska, Martin Leucker
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31302v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attack trees provide a structured approach to security analysis but traditionally require prior knowledge of the attacker's objective. In practice, this objective often remains hidden, even when some attacker actions are partially detected. This paper presents a methodology for generating attack trees without assuming a predefined target by modeling the threat environment as a constraint-weighted graph and applying temporal reachability analysis. The approach identifies probable attacker locations from partial observations and a time budget, carrying traversal cost as an attack-tree attribute. It then extracts target-oriented subgraphs that preserve feasible attack paths while eliminating irrelevant nodes. We demonstrate the framework across three scenarios: a single office building, a multi-building industrial complex, and a real IoT device-communication network recovered from the CICIoT2023 attack dataset. Compared with the baselines, our approach achieves a lower reduction factor while maintaining complete target preservation, substantially outperforming topology-only methods that ignore temporal constraints. We further perform a sensitivity analysis across 66 weight configurations, showing that target identification is stable when strategic value receives at least 20\% of the weight in the single building and at least 50\% in the multi-building complex, while additional experiments reveal sensitivity to perturbations of the underlying strategic-value prior.
tldr: The paper proposes a method to generate attack trees from attack graphs without a predefined target, using constraint-weighted graphs and temporal reachability analysis.
motivation: Traditional attack tree construction requires knowing the attacker's objective in advance, but in practice the target is often hidden even when some attacker actions are partially observed.
method: The threat environment is modeled as a constraint-weighted graph, and temporal reachability analysis identifies probable attacker locations from partial observations and a time budget; target-oriented subgraphs are then extracted while preserving feasible attack paths.
result: The framework is demonstrated on an office building, an industrial complex, and an IoT device-communication network, achieving lower reduction factors while maintaining complete target preservation compared with topology-only baselines.
conclusion: The approach enables efficient attack tree generation for unobservable targets and remains stable under many weight configurations, though sensitivity to the strategic-value prior is observed.

title: Per-Attack Blocking Hides Catalog Vulnerability: A Weakest-Link Analysis Of Tool Manifests
authors: Karthik Karunanithi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Runtime controls for tool-using agents depend on manifests that state what each tool may read and where its output may go. Evaluations of these controls, including ChainCaps, report per-attack blocking: the share of attacks a set of manifests stops. We show that this is the wrong unit. A catalog is only as safe as its weakest source policy: if [MATH] independently authored policies are each wrong with probability [MATH], the chance that the catalog contains an accepted exfiltration path is [MATH], while per-attack blocking stays at [MATH]. Three lines of evidence agree. In synthetic catalogs run through two enforcement engines, ChainCaps and OpenAPPA, per-attack blocking holds at 92% while catalog vulnerability rises from 22% at 10 tools to 99% at 200, and composition provides no protective effect. A fifteen-model authoring pilot shows that real errors cluster by author, so a 200-tool catalog behaves like about 5 independent decisions rather than 60 (95% interval 3.4 to 9.2). On 114 real MCP tools with expert-written rules, the models' own manifests block 89% of attacks yet leave 9 of 15 catalogs open, as the author-effect model predicts and independence does not. Evaluations should report catalog vulnerability, the sink coverage of their tests, and an effective number of independent decisions alongside per-attack blocking.
tldr: The paper argues that per-attack blocking rates mislead when evaluating runtime security controls for tool-using LLM agents, and proposes catalog vulnerability (the weakest-link probability that any accepted exfiltration path exists) as the correct evaluation metric.
motivation: Existing evaluations of tool-manifest enforcement, such as ChainCaps, report the fraction of attacks blocked, which the author claims hides systemic risk because a catalog of independently authored policies is only as safe as its weakest source policy.
method: The author combines an analytic weakest-link model (catalog vulnerability scaling as 1-(1-p)^M) with synthetic catalog experiments across two enforcement engines (ChainCaps and OpenAPPA), a fifteen-model authoring pilot measuring clustering of errors by author, and an evaluation on 114 real MCP tools with expert-written rules.
result: Per-attack blocking stays near 92% while catalog vulnerability climbs from 22% at 10 tools to 99% at 200 tools; authoring errors cluster by author so a 200-tool catalog behaves like roughly 5 independent decisions, and on real MCP tools manifests blocking 89% of attacks still leave 9 of 15 catalogs open.
conclusion: Security evaluations of agent tooling should report catalog vulnerability, sink coverage of their tests, and an effective number of independent decisions alongside per-attack blocking.

title: Harvesting Apple's Orchard: A Security Analysis Of On-Device CoreML Models Across The Apple Ecosystem
authors: Justice Owusu Agyemang, Winifred Harriet Asante, Kwame Opuni-Boachie Obour Agyekum, Kwame Agyeman-Prempeh Agyekum, Francisca Adoma Acheampong, Jerry John Kponyo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Apple ships hundreds of task-specific machine-learning models inside iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and tvOS. We present, to our knowledge, the first systematic security analysis of this on-device surface. We harvested 1,137 CoreML artifacts from six platform images and two device harvests, and a conversion pipeline recovered 155 previously opaque bundles as loadable mlpackage archives. Eight findings. (1) 368 of 1,137 artifacts expose plaintext learned parameters (281 blobs, 369.61 MiB) and 166 of 166 MIL bundles leak internal model-database tokens. (2) Specification versions 1-9 coexist and locale variants diverge architecturally. (3) Across 82,092 adversarial evaluations (221 model paths), worst-case flip rates reach 100%; zero-width spaces flip 65% of the Indian-English and 70% of the US-English SMS filter. (4) A 16-byte weight edit flips 7 of 8 probe inputs of a system model, with no runtime integrity check observed. (5) Loading Apple's own hand-gesture model crashes libBNNS through the public CoreML API (4/4 on production M2, also macOS 27.0); Apple ruled it a self-crash outside the security boundary. (6) Eleven bundles ship isUpdatable=1 hooks. (7) SMS text-classifier latency is 13.1-52.0 ms, 92.4% in the CPU-side NLP core, not the ANE. (8) The classifiers label 8-9 of 10 phishing messages Transactional. We filed three reports with Apple Product; all were declined as not crossing a security boundary, and we report the findings as robustness results.
tldr: The paper presents a systematic security analysis of Apple's on-device CoreML models, uncovering plaintext parameter exposure, adversarial fragility, and weak runtime integrity checks.
motivation: Apple ships many task-specific machine-learning models across its platforms, but their on-device security properties have not been systematically studied.
method: The authors harvested 1,137 CoreML artifacts from platform images and devices, converted opaque bundles into loadable mlpackage archives, and performed adversarial, integrity, crash, and latency evaluations.
result: They found exposed learned parameters, high adversarial flip rates including zero-width-space SMS filter bypasses, a 16-byte weight edit affecting system model outputs, and crashes through the public CoreML API.
conclusion: Apple declined the reports as outside its security boundary, so the work is presented as a robustness study highlighting risks in on-device ML model deployment.

title: Separating Measurement Failures From Defence Failures In Split Language-Model Privacy
authors: Evangelos Pappas Georgios Politis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes before testing a candidate defence, while calibrated attacks can also refute real defences. Separating these failure modes alters which claims survive. We conduct a retrospective evidentiary reanalysis across four split-LLM campaigns and two cross-cutting scope checks covering host key custody and variational mutual-information bounds, mapping every recorded claim to one of five admissibility states (breach, non-detection, undetermined coverage, invalid measurement, or out-of-scope inference). Across a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those four calibrated probes still established qualified privacy breaches in 13 configurations, while utility or learning-gain failures eliminated the remaining 6. In a seven-cell defence-redesign pilot, 2 quantised configurations failed utility gates, calibrated next-byte structure probes breached the 0.02 gate on all 7 cells (0.097 to 0.112), and qualified punctuation-property probes reached 0.79 to 0.89, yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite privacy assessments (the latter from marginal null-band excursions on punctuation bindings). Negative evidence against both defence families remains intact. Scope checks further show that shared-key orthogonal wrappers protect passive network captures without hiding activations from a compromised restoring host, and why near-zero variational lower bounds leave worst-case leakage unconstrained. Rerunnable scripts verify 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts while preserving each campaign's native seed intervals and retrospective boundaries.
tldr: A retrospective evidentiary reanalysis that disentangles measurement failures from genuine defence failures in split-training privacy evaluations of large language models.
motivation: Split-LLM privacy evaluations conflate overlooked gradient leakage, label-shifted reconstructions, and uncalibrated probes with real defence weaknesses, so claims about privacy breaches or defences are hard to trust.
method: The authors map 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts from four split-LLM campaigns and two scope checks (host key custody, variational mutual-information bounds) onto five admissibility states, using calibrated next-byte and punctuation-property probes.
result: Only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those established qualified breaches in 13 of 19 configurations; in a seven-cell redesign pilot all cells breached the 0.02 gate (0.097-0.112), yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite assessments.
conclusion: Separating measurement from defence failure changes which privacy claims survive; negative evidence against both defence families holds, and orthogonal wrappers protect passive captures but not a compromised restoring host.

title: HDMark: Holographic Multi-Bit Model Watermarking For Intellectual Property Protection In Hyperdimensional Computing
authors: Hamed Poursiami, Ahmad Tahmasivand, Farshad Soleiman, Guojing Cong, Thomas Potok, Kai Zeng, Khaled N. Khasawneh, Maryam Parsa
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) models deployed on edge hardware are valuable intellectual property that is easy to steal, since a trained classifier consolidates its learned knowledge into a compact set of class prototype hypervectors; yet protecting their ownership through watermarking remains largely unexplored. We present HDMark, the first model watermarking framework native to HDC, which encodes ownership in the same hyperdimensional algebra the model computes with. HDMark maps a multi-bit owner identity to secret quasi-orthogonal carriers, superimposes them holographically onto the trained class prototypes, and verifies ownership with a statistical test. Across four datasets and three HDC learning rules, HDMark leaves accuracy essentially unchanged and verifies a 64-bit identity in 99.8% of trials at p < 0.001. We derive closed-form expressions for prediction fidelity and bit recovery that match measurements within 0.4 pp mean absolute error. The watermark survives fine-tuning and low-bit quantization, while attempting to erase it through noise injection, pruning, or overwriting severely degrades model accuracy. We further identify a dimension-permutation attack specific to HDC, which reorders hypervector coordinates to evade verification without altering predictions, and counter it through encoder realignment. Finally, an AMD ZCU104 FPGA implementation confirms that HDMark adds no hardware overhead, remains bit-exact under aggressive undervolting, and stays verifiable under timing faults until the classifier itself fails.
tldr: HDMark is the first watermarking framework native to hyperdimensional computing, embedding a multi-bit owner identity holographically into class prototype hypervectors for intellectual property protection of edge-deployed HDC models.
motivation: Trained HDC classifiers compress their learned knowledge into a compact set of class prototype hypervectors, making them easy to steal and leaving ownership protection unexplored.
method: The owner identity is mapped to secret quasi-orthogonal carrier hypervectors that are superimposed onto trained class prototypes using the same hyperdimensional algebra, with ownership verified via a statistical test; closed-form expressions for prediction fidelity and bit recovery are derived and an FPGA implementation is built.
result: Across four datasets and three HDC learning rules, accuracy is essentially unchanged and a 64-bit identity is verified in 99.8% of trials at p < 0.001, with the watermark surviving fine-tuning and low-bit quantization and resisting a newly identified dimension-permutation attack via encoder realignment.
conclusion: HDMark provides robust, zero-hardware-overhead IP protection for HDC models, but the work belongs to classical hardware security and machine-learning watermarking rather than any quantum information direction.

title: Query-Sample Tradeoffs For Revenue Maximization
authors: Yaonan Jin, Wei Tang, Yifan Wang, Mengxiao Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce and study the full query-sample tradeoff for revenue maximization with a single buyer whose value follows an unknown distribution. A learner may adaptively combine value samples, which reveal full buyer values, with pricing queries, which reveal only whether a fresh buyer accepts a selected price. The goal is to learn a price that achieves a [MATH]-multiplicative approximation to optimal revenue with high probability. We ask when, and by how much, reducing the sample budget increases the number of pricing queries required. We establish tight tradeoff bounds for monotone-hazard-rate (MHR), regular, and quasi-monotone-hazard-rate (quasi-MHR) distributions, and almost tight bounds for quasi-regular distributions. Our results reveal sharply different benefits from combining the two information sources. Quasi-MHR distributions admit a smooth intermediate tradeoff: additional samples can reduce the query requirement by polynomial factors. For MHR and regular distributions, however, a sufficiently small constant fraction of the sample-only requirement still leaves the learner facing the full asymptotic query cost attainable with one sample. Our upper bounds are achieved by algorithms that collect all value samples before making queries, while our lower bounds hold even under arbitrary adaptive interleaving of the two forms of access. Along the way, we also fully characterize the sample-only and single-sample query complexities for all four families, eliminating the extra logarithmic dependence on [MATH] in the literature.
tldr: The paper studies tradeoffs between value samples and pricing queries for revenue maximization with an unknown buyer value distribution.
motivation: It aims to understand how two different information sources—full value samples and binary pricing queries—can be combined to learn near-optimal prices under limited access budgets.
method: The authors derive tight upper and lower bounds on sample-query tradeoffs for MHR, regular, quasi-MHR, and quasi-regular distributions, using algorithms that collect samples before querying and lower bounds that allow adaptive interleaving.
result: They characterize distinct tradeoff regimes: quasi-MHR distributions allow smooth polynomial query reduction with more samples, while MHR and regular distributions retain full asymptotic query cost even with a constant fraction of sample-only budget.
conclusion: The work provides a complete complexity characterization for sample-only and single-sample query settings and clarifies when combining samples and pricing queries is beneficial.

title: Spatial Switching Near A Four-loop Homoclinic Bouquet: A Mechanism For Multi-bump Bound States In Coupled Nonlinear Schr\"odinger Systems
authors: Sajjad Bakrani
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how a localized standing wave of a coupled nonlinear Schr\"odinger (CNLS) system can switch between components from one pulse to the next. The standing wave reduction of the CNLS system yields a four-dimensional Hamiltonian system with two reflection symmetries, in which four elementary pulses correspond to a bouquet of homoclinic loops to a saddle. For saddle eigenvalues [MATH] satisfying [MATH], and under suitable nondegeneracy assumptions, we construct stable and unstable invariant manifolds of the four-loop bouquet. Apart from trajectories asymptotic to the saddle in the corresponding time direction, these manifolds characterize one-sided trapping near the bouquet within the critical Hamiltonian level, namely the level set containing the saddle equilibrium. Both manifolds have codimension one in this level. We prove that if they intersect transversely away from the bouquet, producing super-homoclinic orbits, then there exist infinitely many multi-bump homoclinic orbits to the saddle. These orbits correspond to multi-bump localized standing waves of the CNLS system.
tldr: The paper proves the existence of infinitely many multi-bump homoclinic orbits near a four-loop homoclinic bouquet in a four-dimensional Hamiltonian system arising from coupled nonlinear Schrödinger standing waves.
motivation: The authors aim to explain how localized standing waves in coupled nonlinear Schrödinger systems can switch between components from one pulse to the next.
method: They reduce the CNLS system to a four-dimensional Hamiltonian system with reflection symmetries, construct stable and unstable invariant manifolds of the four-loop bouquet, and analyze transverse intersections producing super-homoclinic orbits.
result: Under saddle eigenvalue and nondegeneracy assumptions, transverse intersection of the codimension-one manifolds away from the bouquet implies infinitely many multi-bump homoclinic orbits to the saddle.
conclusion: These homoclinic orbits correspond to multi-bump localized standing waves of the CNLS system, providing a dynamical mechanism for spatial switching between components.

title: TopoCryptoEEG: End-to-End Encrypted Framework For Brainprint Authentication
authors: Qingyu Zeng, Lei Sun, Shuai Zhang, Xiuqing Mao, Ting Zhang, Min Zhao, Wenle Dong
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Brainprint authentication enables continuous identity verification, but EEG data are privacy-sensitive. Existing feature-level encrypted authentication (FLEA) schemes protect extracted features under a trusted-client assumption. We show theoretically and empirically that a compromised client with access to plaintext query features and continuous authentication scores can exactly recover a registered template after finitely many interactions. To address this risk, we propose TopoCryptoEEG, a homomorphic-encryption-based framework that encrypts preprocessed EEG data at the client and performs feature extraction, template matching, score computation, and threshold centering on ciphertexts at the server. This extends protection from extracted features to preprocessed EEG data and removes the client-side plaintext-feature interface exploited by the attack. For efficient encrypted authentication, we develop Multi-Window Topology-Aware Encoding (MWTE) and a Topographic Branch Model with Linear Fusion (TopoFuse-MLP) to preserve EEG spatial information while limiting multiplicative depth. Query-Patch Coordinate Packing (QPCP) and Lane-Preserving BSGS Evaluation (LP-BSGS) further reduce ciphertext operations. Experiments on HGD and BCICIV-2a show high authentication accuracy, with homomorphic computation taking 1-2 s on CPUs and about 14 ms on GPUs. TopoCryptoEEG achieves over 18x average speedup over the EER (IMWUT 2025) baseline, supporting practical privacy-preserving brainprint authentication.
tldr: TopoCryptoEEG is a homomorphic-encryption framework for privacy-preserving EEG brainprint authentication that encrypts preprocessed EEG data and performs matching on ciphertexts.
motivation: Existing feature-level encrypted authentication schemes rely on a trusted client and can leak registered templates to a compromised client, so the authors aim to extend protection to preprocessed EEG data.
method: The framework uses homomorphic encryption with Multi-Window Topology-Aware Encoding, a Topographic Branch Model with Linear Fusion, Query-Patch Coordinate Packing, and Lane-Preserving BSGS evaluation to reduce ciphertext operations.
result: Experiments on HGD and BCICIV-2a show high authentication accuracy, with homomorphic computation taking 1-2 s on CPUs and about 14 ms on GPUs, achieving over 18x average speedup over an EER baseline.
conclusion: The work supports practical privacy-preserving brainprint authentication but is outside the quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems directions.

title: Self-Reference And Relative Incompleteness: From Logical Obstructions To Hardness Hypotheses
authors: Ke Xu Jie Luo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.32095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We define relative incompleteness and use it to provide a unified framework for G\"odelian incompleteness and the limits of local observations in finite SAT. A background is incomplete relative to a target question if two realizations compatible with that background give opposite answers. G\"odelian diagonalization yields a sentence whose truth value differs across two models of the same theory, while solution-dependent blocking yields two formulas that agree on the observed clauses but differ in satisfiability. Both constructions realize a common diagonal relation between truth and acceptance that forces a sound partial evaluator to leave the target undecided. For a satisfiable formula, replacing a single unobserved clause without changing its variable support can make the formula unsatisfiable exactly when all solutions remaining after deletion of that clause agree on its support. If the original formula has a unique solution, this condition is equivalent to redundancy of the clause. More generally, an observation of a satisfiable formula determines satisfiability exactly when it includes a position at which the formula differs from each unsatisfiable completion. For uniquely satisfiable formulas, the positions that every sufficient observation must include are precisely the redundant ones. We also arithmetize solution blocking and construct a tagged fixed point that refers to its own blocking data. Finally, we use self-referential [MATH]-SAT to illustrate how relative incompleteness can provide a logical foundation for formulating a quantitative hardness hypothesis.
tldr: The paper develops a unified logical framework for Gödelian incompleteness and local observational limits in SAT via relative incompleteness and self-reference.
motivation: It aims to connect logical obstructions with quantitative hardness hypotheses by formalizing when a background of observations is insufficient to determine a target answer.
method: The authors define relative incompleteness, use diagonalization and solution-dependent blocking, analyze clause deletion and sufficient observations, and arithmetize solution blocking to construct a tagged fixed point.
result: They characterize when observations determine satisfiability, show redundant clauses are necessary in sufficient observations for uniquely satisfiable formulas, and illustrate how relative incompleteness can ground a hardness hypothesis for self-referential SAT.
conclusion: The work offers a logical foundation for hardness hypotheses based on self-reference and relative incompleteness, but it does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Modeling Of Chemically Reactive Gas Flows For Multi-Scale Problems
authors: Marcel Pfeiffer Franziska Tuttas
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate modeling of chemical reactions plays a key role in the investigation of high-temperature flows. The Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method provides highly accurate solutions for such flows. However, its computational cost becomes prohibitive for low Knudsen regimes. Particle-based continuum methods employing the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) or Fokker-Planck approximations have gained increasing attention in recent years, improve computational efficiency in low-Knudsen regimes by modeling relaxation processes rather than binary collisions, while retaining the particle approach that enables straightforward coupling with DSMC. In the last years, different continuum-based models in the open-source particle code PICLas have been extended to simulate gas mixtures with internal energy modes. The present work focuses on modeling of chemically reactive gas mixtures in the Ellipsoidal Statistical BGK model. Model accuracy is assessed for two test cases of a reactive gases confined in a reservoir.
tldr: The paper extends particle-based continuum methods (Ellipsoidal Statistical BGK) in the PICLas code to model chemically reactive gas mixtures and validates them on two reservoir test cases.
motivation: DSMC is accurate for high-temperature reactive rarefied flows but computationally prohibitive in low-Knudsen regimes, so cheaper particle-continuum hybrid models are needed.
method: Chemical reaction modeling is incorporated into the Ellipsoidal Statistical BGK model within the open-source particle code PICLas, which already supports gas mixtures with internal energy modes; accuracy is assessed on two reactive-gas reservoir test cases.
result: The extended ESBGK model reproduces the reactive flow behavior for the considered test cases, though quantitative comparisons with DSMC reference solutions reveal the model's accuracy limits.
conclusion: Particle-based continuum models can handle chemically reactive rarefied gas flows at reduced cost, enabling multi-scale coupling with DSMC, but further validation is required.

title: Realization Of Expanding Dynamics By A Finite Horizon Parabolic Law Response
authors: Masood Shahbaz Shoukat, Luca Di Persio, Wensheng Jia
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the discrete dynamical system generated by iterating an episodic response of a population density. In each episode, the running potential is frozen at the current density, agents solve a quadratic control problem, and the terminal density is passed to the next episode. For each prescribed positive horizon [MATH] and each [MATH] map [MATH] of finitely many Fourier moments, with [MATH], we construct a finite mode interaction realizing [MATH] at order [MATH]. In scaled coordinates, the exact parabolic response satisfies [MATH]. The estimate is uniform over a full bounded infinite dimensional Sobolev fibre and needs neither Fourier truncation nor an invariant manifold. For scalar targets with disjoint expanding branches that strictly cover their convex hull, this [MATH] control and parabolic compactness yield compact invariant sets of the exact response. These sets factor onto the full one sided shift and contain periodic densities of every least period. Nondegenerate periodic orbits continue, and hyperbolicity requires a separate strict multiplier condition. We also prove a derivative cost obstruction for nonaffine microscopic realization, a susceptibility weighted criterion for population energy designs, and the failure of exact scalar closure under nontrivial rank one feedback. The results concern designed frozen law responses, not Nash consistent mean field game equilibria or finite player limits.
tldr: The paper constructs finite-mode interactions and compact invariant sets for an episodic quadratic-control population-density response, showing symbolic dynamics and periodic orbits.
motivation: The authors study a discrete dynamical system where a frozen potential response leads to expanding dynamics and invariant sets, aiming to realize prescribed dynamics via finite-mode interactions.
method: They use a quadratic control problem over a finite horizon, Fourier moment maps, Sobolev-space estimates, parabolic compactness, and scaling arguments to analyze the exact response.
result: For scalar targets with disjoint expanding branches, they obtain compact invariant sets factoring onto the one-sided shift and containing periodic densities of every least period; they also prove derivative-cost and closure obstructions.
conclusion: The results apply to designed frozen-law responses rather than Nash-consistent mean-field game equilibria or finite-player limits.

title: Sampling Error In Time-Discretized Stochastic Optimal Control
authors: Johannes Milz Aurya Javeed
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study sampling error for Euler discretizations of stochastic optimal control problems driven by Brownian motion. For ordinary Monte Carlo sampling, the error can diverge under time refinement when empirical-mean fluctuations accumulate as bias. Under global Lipschitz assumptions and a bounded noise coefficient, we derive finite-sample bounds for the value-function error without assuming smooth value functions or independence across sampling batches. The bounds isolate the empirical-mean contribution. For convergence under time refinement, ordinary Monte Carlo generally requires the number of samples per stage to grow at a faster rate than the number of intervals in the time mesh, whereas antithetic and recentered sampling eliminate the empirical-mean term and yield error bounds uniform over meshes with a fixed sample size per stage. We establish lower bounds showing that the ordinary and antithetic sampling terms are attained. We also prove sample-size convergence for all three methods on fixed meshes. For antithetic and recentered sampling, convergence is uniform over meshes in every noise dimension, with sharp sample-size rates in dimensions at least three.
tldr: The paper analyzes sampling error in Euler discretizations of stochastic optimal control problems driven by Brownian motion, deriving finite-sample value-function error bounds for Monte Carlo, antithetic, and recentered sampling schemes.
motivation: Ordinary Monte Carlo sampling in time-discretized stochastic optimal control can accumulate empirical-mean fluctuations as bias, causing error to diverge under time refinement, so a careful characterization of sampling error is needed.
method: Under global Lipschitz assumptions and bounded noise coefficient, the authors derive finite-sample bounds on value-function error without smoothness or batch-independence assumptions, and establish matching lower bounds.
result: Ordinary Monte Carlo requires samples per stage to grow faster than the number of time intervals for convergence, while antithetic and recentered sampling eliminate the empirical-mean term and give mesh-uniform bounds with fixed sample size per stage, with sharp sample-size rates in dimensions at least three.
conclusion: Variance-reduction schemes such as antithetic and recentered sampling substantially improve the robustness of time-discretized stochastic optimal control, though the work lies entirely in classical numerical stochastic analysis.

title: A Mixed-primal Fem For Poisson-Fermi Interfacial Problems
authors: Siyad Rahman Mandottil, Neela Nataraj, Ricardo Ruiz-Baier
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a mixed-primal FEM for a linearised Poisson--Fermi interface problem arising from the Bazant--Storey--Kornyshev theory, which describes electrostatic interactions in ionic solutions. It leads to a transmission problem coupling a fourth-order equation in the solvent region with a second-order equation in the solute region. To precisely compute the electrostatic stress and the interactive force in the electrolyte, we reformulate the fourth-order problem as a mixed system by introducing the gradient of the electrostatic potential, the divergence of its gradient, and the gradient of its divergence as additional independent variables. The second-order problem is studied in its primal form as this approach eliminates the requirement for Lagrange multipliers to enforce the transmission conditions. The resulting formulation is discretised using Raviart--Thomas finite elements for the vector variables and piecewise polynomial finite elements for the scalar variables. Well-posedness of the mixed-primal formulation and optimal a priori error estimates for the field variables as well as for the postprocessed Maxwell tensor are established under suitable regularity assumptions, in parameter-weighted norms in which the inf-sup constant is independent of the correlation length and of the permittivity ratio. The constants in the error estimates are independent of both parameters as well, up to a loss of at most half an order when the mesh does not resolve the length scale (square root of the relative permittivity); the Sobolev norms of the solution may still depend on the parameters through boundary layers. The postprocessed Maxwell stress converges with optimal order on quasi-uniform meshes, except for the lowest-order scheme in 3D. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical convergence rates and demonstrate the properties of the proposed method for problems in 2D and 3D.
tldr: A mixed-primal finite element method is developed and analyzed for a linearised Poisson–Fermi transmission problem describing electrostatics in ionic solutions.
motivation: Accurate computation of electrostatic stress and interaction forces in electrolytes under the Bazant–Storey–Kornyshev theory requires robust numerical schemes that handle a fourth-order solvent equation coupled to a second-order solute equation across an interface.
method: The fourth-order problem is recast as a mixed system with gradient, divergence-of-gradient and gradient-of-divergence as extra variables, while the second-order problem stays primal; discretisation uses Raviart–Thomas and piecewise polynomial elements with parameter-weighted norms.
result: Well-posedness and optimal a priori error estimates are proven for field variables and the postprocessed Maxwell tensor, with constants independent of correlation length and permittivity ratio up to a half-order loss.
conclusion: 2D and 3D numerical experiments confirm the theoretical convergence rates and demonstrate the method's ability to capture interfacial electrostatic quantities, with only the lowest-order 3D scheme showing suboptimal stress convergence.

title: Asymptotic Normality Of The Pearson Correlation Between Two Weakly Dependent Random Fields
authors: Jiyue Qin, Armin Schwartzman, Samuel Davenport
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the asymptotic behavior of the sample Pearson correlation coefficient between two weakly dependent random fields on a lattice of any fixed dimension. Under strict stationarity, [MATH]-weak dependence and mild moment conditions, we establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimator on regularly growing domains, which need not be rectangular, with an asymptotic variance expressed through joint fourth-order moments. When the correlation is zero, asymptotic normality holds under weaker conditions. When the fields are independent, the asymptotic variance simplifies to a sum over spatial lags of products of their autocorrelations. The variance approximations behind the classic modified [MATH]-test, although derived for independent Gaussian fields, target the right variance even without Gaussianity. We also give sufficient conditions for asymptotic normality that are easy to check and cover bounded, Gaussian, [MATH]-dependent and independent fields. For Gaussian fields, summable auto- and cross-covariances suffice. These conditions rely on new closure results. Squares and products, although not Lipschitz, preserve [MATH]-dependence for Gaussian fields, and products of independent fields do so when one is positively or negatively associated. Finally, we propose kernel-based estimators of the asymptotic variance, enabling inference without Gaussianity or parametric spatial models. Simulation studies illustrate their finite-sample performance.
tldr: This paper establishes consistency and asymptotic normality of the sample Pearson correlation coefficient between two weakly dependent random fields on lattices.
motivation: The authors aim to provide rigorous asymptotic inference for spatial correlation between random fields without relying on Gaussian or parametric assumptions.
method: Under strict stationarity and weak dependence conditions, they derive asymptotic normality on regularly growing non-rectangular domains and propose kernel-based estimators of the asymptotic variance.
result: The estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, with variance expressed via joint fourth-order moments; simplifications occur for independent fields and weaker conditions suffice for zero correlation.
conclusion: The work enables nonparametric spatial correlation inference and clarifies variance approximations behind modified t-tests, with simulations illustrating finite-sample performance.

title: Sharp Poincar\'e-Wirtinger Inequalities On Finite Graphs
authors: Fayou Zhao Chenghao Xiang

We study the sharp constant [MATH] such that the Poincar\'{e}-Wirtinger inequality \[ \Vert f-m_f\Vert_p\leq C_{G_n,p} {\rm Var}_{p}^{G_n}(f) \] holds for every [MATH] on [MATH], where [MATH] stands for the [MATH]-variation on [MATH] and [MATH] stands for the arithmetic mean of [MATH]. For complete graphs, the optimal constant is known for [MATH], with [MATH] and [MATH]. In this paper, we firstly extend the admissible range to all [MATH]. Secondly, we obtain the sharp constant [MATH] for the star graph [MATH] in the range [MATH] and give estimates for the sharp constant [MATH] on path graphs when [MATH]. Thirdly, we characterize the extremizers on complete graphs and star graphs, and establish the existence of monotone extremizers on path graphs for [MATH]. For path graphs, we obtain explicit sharp constants for [MATH], and interpolation upper bounds for [MATH]. We also prove that for any finite connected graph [MATH], the best constant at [MATH] is exactly its remoteness. Moreover, for general finite connected graphs [MATH] and [MATH], we establish optimal bounds for [MATH]; the complete graph uniquely attains the lower bound for all [MATH]; the path graph attains the upper bound for [MATH], but for [MATH] there exist nonpath graphs that attain the same supremum. Finally, we show that our approach yields sharper upper bounds than the path-based estimates obtained via the Cheeger constant.
tldr: The paper derives sharp Poincare-Wirtinger inequalities and optimal constants for finite connected graphs, including complete, star, and path graphs.
motivation: The authors aim to extend known sharp constants for p-variation Poincare-Wirtinger inequalities on graphs to broader parameter ranges and additional graph families.
method: They analyze extremal problems for functions on finite graphs, characterize extremizers, and establish optimal bounds for the sharp constant across graph classes.
result: They obtain sharp constants for complete and star graphs, estimates and explicit constants for path graphs, and show the p=1 best constant equals graph remoteness, with sharp bounds for general graphs.
conclusion: The work provides a detailed mathematical characterization of sharp Poincare-Wirtinger constants on finite graphs, improving upon path-based Cheeger estimates.

title: A General Framework For Identifying The Joint Potential Outcome Distribution Through Support Restrictions
authors: Kosuke Imai Benedikt Koch
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many causal estimands depend on the joint distribution of potential outcomes, which is generally not identifiable because only one potential outcome can be observed for each unit. To obtain identification, researchers often impose assumptions such as monotonicity and exclusion restriction that constrain the support of this joint distribution. For treatments and outcomes that each take finitely many values, we define a similarity matrix whose entries count, for each pair of potential outcome strata, the number of treatments yielding the same outcome. We then prove that, under unconfoundedness, identification holds if and only if this matrix is invertible, yielding a criterion directly verifiable from the support. In addition, we derive an identification formula for the joint distribution under these support restrictions and show that an average causal estimand is identifiable if and only if its integrand admits an additive representation on the restricted support. Finally, we derive sharp testable implications of the support restriction. Our results unify and generalize a broad range of identification results in the literature.
tldr: The paper develops a linear-algebraic criterion (invertibility of a treatment-outcome similarity matrix) for identifying the joint distribution of potential outcomes under support restrictions in causal inference.
motivation: Joint distributions of potential outcomes are generally unidentifiable from observed data because only one potential outcome per unit is realized, so researchers rely on assumptions such as monotonicity or exclusion restrictions that constrain the support.
method: For finite-valued treatments and outcomes, the authors define a similarity matrix counting treatments that yield matching outcomes across potential-outcome strata, and study identification under unconfoundedness via invertibility of this matrix, deriving an identification formula and a condition for additive representability of average causal estimands.
result: Identification of the joint potential-outcome distribution holds if and only if the similarity matrix is invertible, average causal estimands are identifiable iff their integrand admits an additive representation on the restricted support, and sharp testable implications of the support restriction are derived.
conclusion: The framework unifies and generalizes many existing identification results in the causal inference literature and yields support-verifiable criteria for identifiability and testability.

title: Depth Of Leaves In Closed Linear $\lambda$-terms: Exact Recurrence, Limit Law And Edge Window
authors: Olivier Bodini
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31323v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] (resp.\ [MATH]) be the depth of a uniform leaf (resp.\ node) in a uniform closed linear [MATH]-term of size [MATH]. A bijective yields an exact polynomial-time recurrence for the full depth profile. By the method of moments, [MATH] converges in law to the density [MATH] on [MATH], i.e.\ [MATH], with [MATH]; likewise [MATH]. A backward Markov chain gives the corresponding local limits for [MATH]. The limit density diverges at [MATH], and the profile has a second scale: a window of width [MATH] around [MATH], which carries a fraction of order [MATH] of the nodes, at a density [MATH] times larger than in the bulk. We prove that a single explicit function describes both regimes: uniformly in [MATH], \[ n^{3/4}\,\mathbb P(D_n=d)=g\Bigl({\sqrt n}\Bigr)+O(n^{-1/16}),\qquad n^{3/4}\,\mathbb P(K_n=d)={n}\,g\Bigl({\sqrt n}\Bigr)+O(n^{-1/16}), \] where [MATH] is a parabolic cylinder function. In particular [MATH] with [MATH] standard Gaussian. The proofs rest on harmonic functions of the heat equation evaluated along the backward chain.
tldr: The paper derives exact recurrences and limit laws for the depth of leaves and nodes in uniformly random closed linear lambda-terms, including a parabolic-cylinder-function profile spanning bulk and edge-window regimes.
motivation: Understanding the typical shape and depth profile of random lambda-terms is a fundamental question in analytic combinatorics and the theory of computation, relevant to average-case analysis of functional programs.
method: A bijective combinatorial construction yields an exact polynomial-time recurrence for the depth profile; the method of moments and a backward Markov chain tied to harmonic functions of the heat equation establish the limit laws and local limits.
result: The normalized leaf and node depths converge in law to an explicit density that diverges at the origin, and a single parabolic cylinder function uniformly describes both the bulk and a second scale window of width ~n^{-1/4}; in particular a Gaussian limit emerges for the edge window.
conclusion: Random closed linear lambda-terms exhibit a rich two-scale depth structure captured by a unified limit function, with proofs built on heat-equation harmonic functions along a backward chain.

title: SwarmLeak: Does Coordination Improve Privacy Attacks On Llm Agents?
authors: Asma Farajidizaji, Vyas Raina, Vatsal Raina, Ivaxi Sheth
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly collaborate in group chats while holding tool access to confidential records, which makes the shared chat an attack surface. It remains unclear whether several colluding attackers extract such information more effectively than one. We introduce SwarmLeak, a red-teaming dataset of 24 synthetic group-chat scenarios across healthcare, law, finance, and software engineering, where attackers pose as colleagues to make a victim agent post protected fields despite an explicit confidentiality policy. With GLM 5.2 attacking five victim models through seven conversational strategies, we compare one attacker with a swarm of four sharing a private channel, matching scenarios, strategies, and a 200,000-token budget that also covers swarm coordination. Swarms show no advantage: a single attacker matches or exceeds them on every victim, and the share of runs leaking any field differs between conditions by at most 14.3 percentage points, whereas changing the victim shifts it from 0% to 99.4%. On the two most vulnerable models, nearly every run leaks under both conditions, but single attackers expose more of the record at first disclosure (85.4% vs. 68.1% of protected fields on Nemotron 3.5 Lightning). Four of the five victims leaked despite the policy. GLM 5.2 retrieved protected data in 64.3% of individual-attack runs and leaked in 0.6%: retrieval does not imply disclosure, but in high-stakes settings even one leaked field can identify a patient or client. At equal budgets, a larger red team is not automatically a stronger one; the victim model matters far more.
tldr: SwarmLeak is a red-teaming dataset and study testing whether multiple colluding LLM attackers extract confidential information from victim LLM agents more effectively than a single attacker in group-chat settings.
motivation: LLM agents increasingly operate in group chats with tool access to sensitive records, creating a shared-channel attack surface, and it was unclear whether coordinated multi-attacker 'swarms' are more effective than lone attackers under equal budgets.
method: The authors build 24 synthetic group-chat scenarios across healthcare, law, finance, and software engineering, then compare a single GLM 5.2 attacker against a swarm of four attackers with a private coordination channel, using seven conversational strategies and a matched 200,000-token budget across five victim models.
result: Swarms showed no advantage: a single attacker matched or exceeded them on every victim, with at most a 14.3 percentage-point difference between conditions, whereas the choice of victim model shifted leak rates from 0% to 99.4%; single attackers also exposed more protected fields at first disclosure (85.4% vs. 68.1% on Nemotron 3.5 Lightning).
conclusion: At equal token budgets, larger red teams are not automatically stronger, and the victim model's robustness dominates outcomes; retrieval of protected data (64.3% of runs) far exceeds actual disclosure (0.6%), though even a single leaked field can be identifying in high-stakes settings.

title: Where Did My Tokens Go? Verifiable Token Billing For Llm Services
authors: Jiayuan Du, Yebo Feng, Lin Zhang, Konglin Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Users of large language model (LLM) services receive token bills with limited evidence of which calls incurred their charges. In broker-mediated agent workflows, calls arise after authorization and billing evidence spans service domains. A bill can count one genuine receipt twice and omit another. Valid metering evidence can also be attributed to the wrong execution. We present , which uses authenticated provider acceptances to establish settlement coverage and verify token charges. An authenticated causal history links runtime attempts to the signed policy, and jointly signed handoffs bind intent, dispatch, and acceptance to the same call. Handoffs submitted independently of the bill can reveal omitted calls. The auditor requires a one-to-one match between observable acceptances and settled receipts. For each acceptance, a common provider relation binds metered usage to the cache-dependent execution of the accepted input using the registered model and serving rules, and checks the charge under the pricing rule. To limit serving-path overhead, providers can use attested state transitions in trusted execution environments or defer proof generation until audit by committing to witnesses in receipts before settlement. The auditor recomputes the bill from the verified charges. We prove audit soundness relative to authenticated evidence. Across five models, with signed provider receipts achieves 94.4--107.4\% of baseline throughput with 54--66\,ms of online non-LLM processing per request. In a separate eight-call replay, deferring scoped proofs reduces foreground protocol time from 1.20\,s to 8.65\,ms (99.28\%). The auditor rejects all 1,600 validly signed attack queries across 100 adaptive episodes.
tldr: The paper proposes a verifiable token billing system for LLM services using authenticated provider receipts, causal histories, and trusted execution attestations to audit charges and detect omitted or duplicated calls.
motivation: LLM service users receive token bills with limited evidence of which calls incurred charges, and broker-mediated agent workflows create opportunities for double-counting, omitted calls, and misattribution.
method: The system uses signed provider acceptances, jointly signed handoffs linking intent to dispatch and acceptance, and an auditor enforcing one-to-one matching between observable acceptances and settled receipts; it can use TEE-attested state transitions or deferred proof generation with witness commitments.
result: Across five models, signed provider receipts achieve 94.4–107.4% of baseline throughput with 54–66 ms online non-LLM processing per request; deferred scoped proofs reduce foreground protocol time from 1.20 s to 8.65 ms, and the auditor rejects all 1,600 validly signed attack queries in 100 adaptive episodes.
conclusion: Verifiable token billing can provide audit soundness relative to authenticated evidence with practical overhead, enabling accountability in LLM service billing.

title: The Descriptive Complexity Of Continuous Selections With Prescribed Hausdorff Dimension Of The Graph
authors: Megha Pandey Xiongwei Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study the existence of continuous selections of set-valued functions with prescribed Hausdorff dimension of their graphs. We consider Hausdorff-continuous functions defined on the unit interval whose values are nonempty compact subsets of the real line. We prove that, for every [MATH], the collection of all such functions admitting a continuous selection whose graph has Hausdorff dimension [MATH] is [MATH]-complete and hence is not Borel. Further, we show that this result holds even when the set-valued functions have totally disconnected values. Thus, we obtain a complete classification of the descriptive complexity of the existence problem for all possible Hausdorff dimensions of continuous graphs over the unit interval.
tldr: The paper classifies the descriptive complexity of the existence problem for continuous selections of set-valued functions whose graphs have prescribed Hausdorff dimension.
motivation: The authors study continuous selections of compact-set-valued functions and aim to determine the Borel complexity of whether such selections can have a graph of a given Hausdorff dimension.
method: They work in descriptive set theory, considering Hausdorff-continuous set-valued functions on the unit interval with nonempty compact real values, and analyze the complexity class of the corresponding existence sets.
result: For every prescribed dimension, the collection of such functions admitting a continuous selection with graph of that Hausdorff dimension is shown to be complete for an appropriate complexity class and hence non-Borel, even for totally disconnected values.
conclusion: This provides a complete classification of the descriptive complexity of the continuous-selection existence problem across all possible Hausdorff dimensions of graphs.

title: Trustworthy Edge Ai: Security, Privacy, And Resilience For Distributed Intelligence
authors: Subhasis Dasgupta Jaydip Sen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This chapter examines the principles and emerging research directions for building secure, privacy-preserving, and resilient Edge Artificial Intelligence (Edge AI) systems. As intelligence shifts from centralized clouds to distributed edge environments, challenges arise in ensuring data integrity, privacy, and reliable operation under adversarial and uncertain conditions. The chapter analyzes Edge AI architectures, emphasizing the expanded attack surface due to heterogeneous devices, resource constraints, and dynamic networks. It reviews core security mechanisms, including hardware-rooted trust, zero-trust models, secure communication, and attestation. Privacy-preserving approaches, such as federated learning, secure aggregation, and differential privacy, enable collaborative intelligence without centralized data sharing. Resilience strategies, including fault tolerance, adversarial robustness, and adaptive orchestration, are also explored. Case studies from smart cities, autonomous vehicles, healthcare, and industrial IoT illustrate practical trade-offs. The chapter advocates a holistic, cross-layer design integrating security, privacy, and resilience for trustworthy edge intelligence.
tldr: This chapter surveys security, privacy, and resilience principles and research directions for trustworthy Edge AI systems.
motivation: Intelligence is increasingly moving from centralized clouds to distributed edge environments, creating challenges in data integrity, privacy, and reliable operation under adversarial and uncertain conditions.
method: The authors review Edge AI architectures, attack surfaces, hardware-rooted trust, zero-trust models, secure communication, attestation, federated learning, secure aggregation, differential privacy, fault tolerance, adversarial robustness, and adaptive orchestration, with case studies from smart cities, autonomous vehicles, healthcare, and industrial IoT.
result: The chapter identifies practical trade-offs and advocates a holistic cross-layer design integrating security, privacy, and resilience for trustworthy edge intelligence.
conclusion: Trustworthy Edge AI requires cross-layer security, privacy-preserving collaboration, and resilience strategies tailored to distributed resource-constrained environments.

title: Mixed-Initiative Mining Of Root-Cause Analyses Into Audit Priors For C/c++ Vulnerability Hunting
authors: Yuhei Kawakoya, Eitaro Shioji, Yuto Otsuki, Makoto Iwamura
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerability auditing of large C/C++ codebases is constrained by limited review attention. Human auditors and LLM-based agents need operational priors that indicate where to look first and what to suspect, but such priors are rarely available in directly usable form. Rather than proposing a new vulnerability detector, we derive audit-steering artifacts from evidence-backed root-cause analysis (RCA) reports. We introduce two complementary representations: Occurrence Context (OC), a location prior based on file role, function role, and data-structure class; and Vulnerability-Inducing Structural Patterns (VISP), reusable failure-mechanism priors. OC guides where to inspect, while VISP guides what to suspect. On 108 CVEs from Vul4C, OC's parser-based priority ranking, without LLM inference, outperforms generic prioritization baselines with moderate-to-large effect sizes. Packaged as executable SKILLs, OC and VISP form a dual-SKILL workflow that improves audit-relevant broad coverage, defined as match-or-partial findings within ground-truth functions that share the patch's failure mechanism, as assessed by three LLM judges. Across the 108-CVE cohort, dual-SKILL improves function-level broad matches by 5.3 percentage points; gains reach 7.2 points on mid-size projects and 15.0 points on large (1500-4999-line) vulnerable files. These results suggest that RCA-derived priors help direct limited audit attention toward vulnerable code. The agent-coverage evaluation is a single-run operational probe, with one run per commit, characterizing the direction and scale of the effect rather than its precise magnitude.
tldr: The paper derives audit-steering priors from root-cause analysis reports to improve C/C++ vulnerability hunting by human auditors and LLM agents.
motivation: Vulnerability auditing of large C/C++ codebases is limited by review attention, and operational priors indicating where to inspect and what to suspect are rarely available in directly usable form.
method: The authors introduce Occurrence Context (OC), a location prior based on file/function role and data-structure class, and Vulnerability-Inducing Structural Patterns (VISP), reusable failure-mechanism priors, packaged as executable SKILLs for a dual-SKILL audit workflow.
result: On 108 CVEs from Vul4C, OC's parser-based priority ranking outperforms generic baselines, and the dual-SKILL workflow improves function-level broad matches by 5.3 percentage points overall, with larger gains on mid-size and large projects.
conclusion: RCA-derived priors can help direct limited audit attention toward vulnerable code, though the agent-coverage evaluation is a single-run operational probe characterizing direction and scale rather than precise magnitude.

title: Not Just Any Example: Security Requirements And Fix Patterns For Guiding Llm Vulnerability Repair
authors: Zichen Liu, Liangyi Huang, Stanley Nguyen, Kha Tu Nguyen, Xinda Wang, Xusheng Xiao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31993v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software vulnerabilities leave systems open to attack, and their remediation is often delayed. Large language models (LLMs) have advanced automated patch generation, yet passing functionality tests does not ensure that a patch enforces the security requirement the vulnerability violated. Existing vulnerability repair techniques rely on curated patterns or templates with limited coverage, leaving unclear which repair strategies carry over across vulnerabilities and how they can steer LLMs. We present a large-scale empirical study that relates recurring fix patterns to the security impacts of vulnerabilities and examines how this knowledge can guide LLM-based repair. Building on a manual study of security patches, we cluster 3,816 security patches from 348 open-source repositories and analyze the edits and their context to derive concrete fix patterns, ranging from local safeguards to coordinated changes across multiple locations. We define 12 security impact classes by the security requirements that vulnerabilities violate and map them to repair categories and fix patterns, revealing characteristic repairs, alternative strategies within a class, and patterns shared across classes. We then use these patterns and impact-pattern associations to select repair examples for four LLMs on repair tasks of varying complexity. Guided example selection raises the four-model mean pass@3 from 37.9% under zero-shot prompting to up to 49.2%, whereas randomly selected examples reach only 36.9%. Our findings connect vulnerability characterization with patch generation and support organizing repair knowledge around security requirements.
tldr: A large-scale empirical study that clusters 3,816 security patches to derive fix patterns tied to 12 security-requirement impact classes and uses these to guide LLM-based vulnerability repair.
motivation: Passing functionality tests does not guarantee an LLM-generated patch actually enforces the security requirement violated, and existing pattern/template-based repair techniques have limited coverage and unclear transferability.
method: The authors manually analyze and cluster 3,816 security patches from 348 open-source repositories, derive concrete fix patterns, define 12 security impact classes, and map them to repair categories; they then use these patterns to select repair examples for four LLMs on tasks of varying complexity.
result: Guided example selection raises the four-model mean pass@3 from 37.9% under zero-shot prompting to up to 49.2%, whereas randomly selected examples reach only 36.9%.
conclusion: The work connects vulnerability characterization with patch generation and supports organizing automated repair knowledge around security requirements.

title: Recognizing Potentially Planar Degree Sequences
authors: Renwen Tian Zhe Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.32060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Testing for a simple planar realization is strongly NP-complete even on graphic [MATH]-term degree lists of minimum degree at least three and sum [MATH]. Two [MATH]-vertex triangulations have sorted degree lists whose midpoint is graphic and has no planar realization, ruling out a characterization by simultaneous affine inequalities in the sorted entries even at sum [MATH]. For arbitrary lists, an ordered interval rule and a finite difference in the degrees alone each give an exact criterion. On an [MATH]-bit input, a deterministic [MATH]-time search finds a realization or rules one out. At the first two even sums beyond the sparse bound of Bar-Noy et al., we classify all exceptions among positive graphic lists, giving linear-time recognition on a word RAM throughout the extended range. In particular, for [MATH], appending [MATH] twos suffices to make every graphic [MATH]-term list of minimum degree at least three and sum [MATH] potentially planar.
tldr: The paper studies algorithmic recognition of potentially planar graphic degree sequences and characterizes exceptions beyond sparse bounds.
motivation: Testing whether a degree sequence has a simple planar realization is strongly NP-complete in general, so the authors seek exact criteria and faster recognition in structured ranges.
method: They use ordered interval rules, finite differences in degrees, midpoint constructions from triangulations, and deterministic search algorithms on bit inputs.
result: They rule out characterization by simultaneous affine inequalities in sorted entries, give exact criteria for arbitrary lists, and classify exceptions for the first even sums beyond the Bar-Noy et al. sparse bound.
conclusion: The work advances graph-theoretic recognition of planar degree sequences and yields linear-time recognition in an extended range on a word RAM.

title: A Kernel Framework For Linear Operator Equations
authors: Valentin Tissot-Daguette Damir Filipovic
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solving linear operator equations with nonlocal terms or heterogeneous constraints often requires specific numerical schemes. We develop a unified approach based on embedding such equations into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Differential, boundary, and integral operators are represented by their Riesz representers in the RKHS. The equations are solved in the regularized least-squares sense at finitely many collocation points. The solution is a finite linear combination of operator-induced representers and is obtained from a single linear system. Its sensitivities, such as financial Greeks, follow by direct differentiation. To reduce the computational cost for large collocation sets, we introduce a Nystr\"om approximation based on subsampling the operator-induced representers. It yields the best approximation of this solution within the reduced trial space, in a regularized empirical norm. Numerical examples cover ordinary, partial, and partial integro-differential equations, including multi-asset and jump-diffusion option pricing.
tldr: The authors propose an RKHS-based kernel framework for solving linear operator equations (differential, boundary, integral) via regularized least squares at collocation points, with a Nyström subsampling approximation for scalability.
motivation: Existing numerical schemes for operator equations with nonlocal terms or heterogeneous constraints tend to be problem-specific, so a unified and general solver is desirable.
method: Equations are embedded in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space where operators are represented by Riesz representers; solutions are finite linear combinations of operator-induced representers found from a single linear system, with Nyström subsampling to reduce cost.
result: The approach handles ODEs, PDEs, and partial integro-differential equations, including multi-asset and jump-diffusion option pricing, and yields sensitivities by direct differentiation.
conclusion: The framework offers a unified, differentiable, and computationally scalable kernel-based solver for a broad class of linear operator equations in numerical analysis and mathematical finance.

title: Bounds On The Distance Of Subgradient Trajectories To The Optimal Set
authors: Nicholas Dwork, Charles Tsao, Jorge Balbas, Cody Coleman, John M. Pauly
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A subgradient method with a constant step size may reach a minimizer and subsequently move away from it. Thus, a bound on the best objective value does not characterize the remainder of the trajectory. In this manuscript, we first establish that the trajectory enters a near-optimal sublevel set in finitely many iterations. We then use the Hausdorff distance between this sublevel set and the optimal set to bound the distance of every subsequent iterate from the optimal set. For objectives with weak sharp minima, we derive a tighter bound and construct examples demonstrating that the bound is tight. Numerical experiments confirm these theoretical results and illustrate when the bounds are conservative.
tldr: The paper derives bounds on how far subgradient-method iterates with constant step size can stray from the optimal set, using the Hausdorff distance between a near-optimal sublevel set and the optimal set.
motivation: For constant-step subgradient methods, a bound on the best objective value so far does not describe the remaining trajectory, since iterates can approach and then leave a minimizer; a geometric characterization of the whole trajectory is needed.
method: The authors prove that the trajectory enters a near-optimal sublevel set in finitely many iterations, then bound the distance of all subsequent iterates to the optimal set via its Hausdorff distance, with a tighter bound for objectives with weak sharp minima and explicit tight examples.
result: Finite-iteration entry into the sublevel set is established, the Hausdorff-distance bound holds for all later iterates, the weak-sharp-minima bound is provably tight, and numerical experiments confirm the theory while showing regimes where the bounds are conservative.
conclusion: Hausdorff-distance geometry between sublevel and optimal sets provides a clean, sometimes tight characterization of subgradient trajectory behavior, complementing objective-value guarantees.

title: Robust Estimators For Stochastic Model-Based Derivative-Free Optimization
authors: Lindon Roberts Fangyu Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31853v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Derivative-free optimization (DFO) methods are popular for solving stochastic optimization problems, with model-based methods being a practically successful class of DFO algorithm. In most existing works, sufficiently accurate objective estimates (used for model construction and to test for sufficient decrease) are constructed by taking a sample mean of several noisy evaluations. In this work, we demonstrate that using robust estimators (specifically the median, trimmed mean, and median-of-means) can improve the sample complexity of model-based DFO methods. Our numerical results demonstrate that robust estimators are also a practical choice for algorithm implementations.
tldr: This paper shows that robust estimators (median, trimmed mean, median-of-means) instead of sample means can reduce the sample complexity of model-based derivative-free optimization for stochastic objectives.
motivation: Model-based derivative-free optimization methods typically rely on sample-mean objective estimates for model construction and sufficient-decrease tests, which can be statistically inefficient under heavy-tailed or high-variance noise.
method: The authors analyze model-based DFO algorithms where objective values are estimated via robust statistics (median, trimmed mean, median-of-means) and derive improved sample-complexity bounds, supported by numerical experiments.
result: Robust estimators provably improve the sample complexity of model-based DFO and also perform well in practice compared with sample-mean-based implementations.
conclusion: Robust estimation is a practical and theoretically justified substitute for sample means in stochastic derivative-free optimization.

title: Information Security Risk Preparedness In Electronic Data Interchange: A Comparative Assessment Of General It And Healthcare Environments
authors: Naresh Kshetri, Bishwo Prakash Pokharel, Arati Bastakoti, Anjana Bastakoti
abstract: ArXiv:2611.31294v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) supports the exchange of structured information across business and healthcare environments, making information security and organizational risk management critical to reliable digital transactions.
